WTIVN.E UP, ENGLAND!!
A GREAT INTERNATIONAL and UNIVERSAL EXIIIBITION is to be held in GHENT in 1913 in which Great Britain cannot afford not to be
represented officially.

Belgium is our best Continental Customer, comparatively with the size of the Ceuntry. Ghent is admirably situated on the main road from the Continent to England. Every nation alike will be ready to come to the neutral ground of Belgium for this great exhibition. Already the Gerlllllll Committee, ever alert to seize the passing opportunity, encouraged by their sale at Brusfells, 1910, has signed an agreement to con- struct a special pavilion, which will be one of the most striking points of the Exhibition. The Congress of the United States of America that refused to contribute to the Brussels Exhibition has, at the request of President Taft, consented to exhibit officially at Ghent. The Government of Greece the same. France, with characteristic enterprise, is taking twice as much space as she had in Brussels, and is asking for more. Italy will have a fine Official Exhibit. The Canadian Government has secured a prominent position for an Official Exhibition. Negotiations are on the point of termination with Russia. The far- off countries of China and Japan, Chili, Peru, Brazil, and Cuba, the Argentine Republic, New Zealand and India will all be there. EXHIBIT OR LOSE THE TRADE.

WHITE LEGHORNS. These are the subject of this week's illustration, but they are by no means the only colour in Leghorns. We have black, brown, duckwing, pile, blue and buff. The whites are, however, the most popular as a utility fowl, followed closely by the blacks. Indeed some people claim that these latter are even better layers than the whites. They may possibly lay a few more eggs, but they are not so large, and of course a large egg finds a more ready market than a small one. That is why I give premier place to the whites. They ago grand layers of large white shelled eggs, and what- ever colour you choose, so big as it bears the name Leghorn, you are assured of a full egg basket.

rn the "Feathered World." The late Mr. flichardscn (lecturer to the Cheshire County Council) used to say "That in all his experi- ments with various breeds, be found none to equal the white Leghorn for egg production." Leghorns are profitable inasmuch as they are very small eaters and good foragers, thus costing very little to keep. And when they are given a free grass range, they need very little but a good daily feed of sound grain. They also stand confinement well, and if provided with plenty of scratching material, they are quite content. This they must have to satisfy their active nature. PAY OLD CITICI:ES TILIDE.

I have been requested by one of my readers to write a few lints on this branch of p-ultry farming. First of all he wants some information on how to start in a small way. Of cruise, without any knowledge at all it would be foolish to attempt doing big things. I will therefore deal with the subject as it affects those in a similar position to that of my inquirer. His space is somewhat limited, and I should say that he could nct accommodate more than two pens of stock birds. First of all we must consider local surround- ings. What are the class of customers likely to be in and near our locality? And then, what breeds are most likely to find ready sale? Taking into considera- tion the fact, that we must so sell our produce as to build up a griod connection of customers, this means that the quality and pedigree of the stock must be cf the best. Very well then, let us make a start.

div.p: LOC.\ f, SI: EROCTSDINGS.

The class of customers in and around this part are likely to be farmers, cottagers, suburban poultry farmers and backyarders. Therefore you will at once observe that the demand will be for general utility stock. Remember also that I have already pointed out that your space is limited to two pens. Theie- fore again, you must decide on what breeds should occupy these two Fens. Seeirg that we have con- cluded that the dersand will be for utility birds, and there are so many good utility breeds to select from, a difficulty arises as to which are best. It is not neccessary in this instance that they shall be pure breeds and I would strongly advise the mating of the two following crosses : Houdan—White Leghorn and Houdan Orpington,Buil or White according to choice. No from these two pens you would produce both good winter and summer laying pullets, and further the cockerels from either pen would make very accept- able table Mids. Such matings would certainly produce stock that wruld always demand a ready sale. The peat point to consider and which my readers especially desire to know is, whether to start with DROOOIE9 on IN( Ufl.ll'ollS.

By all means when making a start on the foregoing lines, I would certainly recommend broody hens The initial outlay would be less and in all probability you would find ready customers within easy distance, so that the further expense of packing ano dispatching the chicks would be obviated. Still further, it is always advisable that you sM uld make a start with methods easily understood rather than by taking a plunge into the more difficult operation of dealing in clay old chicks by the incubator process. You could merge into the latter as you gained experience and as your capital grew. You may ask : How am Ito be assured of a regular stock of broodies ? " 1 quite admit that the egg average from the two pens would be greater than you could cope with by setting all the eggs laid. Of course it was never meant, and I hope never expected that this should be so. The object should be to have not less than five broodies sitting at one time. And as soon as they hatch out the batches should be made up into twelve chicks with the ben. These should be sold cff without delay, five more broodies acquired and set accordingly. Now Ido not think you would hvve very much difficulty in obtain- ing the requisite amount of broody hens. Of course you would have to "stir yourself." Get round the farmers, offer a decent figure for broodies, leave a stamped postcard and ask them to notify you when they have any on stock. You would sodn get plenty of broodies.

div.head: VALI. fl OF ST ,(K.
div.p: VALI. fl OF ST ,(K.

The next point is, what price should be asked for a ben and twelve chicks? I never like fixing prices for anyone, one is always apt to make mistakes. But in these days of minimums it will be quite safe if I name a price which should not be lowered, taking into consideration that my desire is for y, u to make your operations profitable. In the first place you will often have to pay as much as 4s. for the broody ben, and when you come to re-sell you can never get the original value. So that if you sell her with twelve chicks for Bs. you would then be asking at the rate of sixpence per chick and 2s. for the hen. They are worth this, and you should find little difficulty in obtaining these prices. If you do, then give up the day old chicken trod° as unprofitable. Don't let me forget to state that all surplus eggs could be sold for sitting purposes. This would be another means of income, and would help to provide an immediate turnover for the purchasing of broodiee and food for your stock. Once you have got a good connection for the sale of day old chicks, you would find that this Branch of poultry farming is most profitable. If you have any further questions to ask I am at your service. Send those queries along please !

div.head: SEASONABLE NOTES.
div.p: SEASONABLE NOTES.

Get as many eggs down as you possibly can from the heavy hrceds this month. Thus you will be assured of laying stcck for next winter. You may also commence to set eggs [from the lighten varieties, if you have not already begun. Once a week at the time of the year a little Epsom salts should be added to the drinking water, and once a week a small piece of sulphate of iron, about the size of a hazel nut, to every quart of drinking water, this will help to keep the breeding stock in good healthy condition. Pay attention to early chicks, and ccca,ionally examine them for vermin. If any are detected, give the chicks a good dusting with Keatings Powder. The latter is very efficacious, and a most useful commodity to have by you. On fine days let the youngsters have as much open run as you possibly can, but when the days are cold and windy keep diem in the covered run. Keep them active by burying a few handfuls of dry chick food in the scratching shed. Don't forget the sprouted oats they are much enjoyed by the chicks, besides they are a most nourishing 'diet.

div.head: rilE STOCK
div.p: rilE STOCK

Give the cccupants of the breeding pens plenty of nourishing food. At night time you should separi.we • the male bird and give him an extra feed of maize about three times a week, and a few pieces of lean meat also. This will aid him in keeping vigorous, and the trouble of doing so will well repay sou. For when the male bird is underfed, what else can you expect but infertility. All these little hints, observed and carried out, pay well foi the work involved.

div.head: EGGS FOG SITTING PURPOSES.
div.p: EGGS FOG SITTING PURPOSES.
'When selecting eggs for sitting purposes, see that none are cracked or badly shaped. Use only those of moderate size and of a good shape, and hard shelled.

Insurance Commissioners desire to call the attention of those terming approved societies and of persons applying for membership to the facilities afforded under the Insurance Act, for obtaining birth certificates at a fee of Cd., instgad of at the usual fee of 3s. 7d. Every person, therefore, who wishes to obtain a certificate of his birth in order to apply for membership, should fill up the form and apply to the Superintendent Registrar or Registrar, of the district where his birth is registered. He will then obtain the certificate for 61. The :form in which the application must be made can be obtained from any Superintendent Registrar or Registrar, but the certifi- cate can only be granted by the Superintendent Registrar or Registrar having the custody of the register in which the birth is registered. it the application for the certificate is made by post, a stamped and addressed envelope must be enclosed,

Continuing Mr D3bsou said it was an 91d and true saying that " prevention is better than cure." The principal of the Insurance Act was the prevention as well at the cure of sickness. (Applause.) Take the case of consumption. What a terrible thing that was that one out of every nine persons in the country was doomed to die of that white scourge, consumption. Nearly as many people as there were in Warrington, 75,000 died from this plague every year. Every year that number was demanded as victims of that fell disease. That would be bad enough if consumption were the disease they htld all along been consider- ing it to be—an hereditary disease. Medical men had however said that by reason of their re.earchee consumption was not what the people had imagined it to be. They said that where the children of a consumptive father or mother, or both, contracted that disease, it was not because of their hereditary nature, but because the children had been brought into contact with the diseased persons. It was because they had been subjected to the same insanitary environment their parents had and had to suffer from lack of food as the parents bad done. The doctors said that if we would only do something for people suffering from the early stages of the disease— get them isolated from their families—there was no earthly reason why, in the course of a generation or so, they should not stamp out, as efficiently as they had stamped out small-pox, that terrible disease, consump- tion. (Applause) How would the Act act in I that particular direction? The Government had provided out of the State funds— not out of the people's weekly contributione— the sum of £1,000,000 and with that money there were to be erected in various parts of the country sinatoria. Those buildings would be equipped on the most up-to- date lines in every respect and superintended by medical men who had specialised on that disease. We now stood a good chance of having the disease removed for ever. It would be worth all the worry, trouble and expense it had so far entailed. (Hear' hear.) If any of the members under the Act should be seen suffering from the early stages of the disease they would have the privileee of going into these sanatorias not as an act of charity but as a right for which they had worked and paid. (Hear, hear.) As to the preventive nature of the Act, they had been for a long time past placing various measures on the Statute Book with is view to remedy- ing the evils which existed through

INSANITARY DWELLINGS AND SLUM PROPERTY especially in some of the largor manufacturing towns in the North of England. Up to the present be was zorry to say all of those Acts bad been inoperative. All sorts of reasons had been produced for it and one was, that he thought there was something in the state. meat that to a large extol: it was due to the indifference on the part of the ratepayers in electing on their Boards, Borough and District and Cannty Councils, men who were interested in that class of property and who were ownera of that property and would never raise a finger but would stop those Acts from coming into operation. (Hear, hear and applause.) Some of them might wonder what bearing that had on the Insurance Act, but there was a clause in the Act which stated that if the members of a friendly society should notice that undue or excessive demands were being made for sick payments from dwellers in a certain locality or workers in a certain factory or anywhere where they had reason to suspect the water supply or other conditions, they would have sent down from London, inspectors who would hold an inquiry. If it could be found that those increased calls for sidk benefits were due to the water supply or bad property, they could call on the owner to make good the loss to the friendly society for paying those extra payments. (Hear, hear and applause). Then the third point as to the preventive nature of the Act. History had taught them beyond the possibility of a doubt that a country that was diminishing in population soon became a decaying country. Spain at one time had 25,000,000 of a population but now it wal only 15,000,000 France also would soon be classed in the category or decaying rations. Ireland at one time had eight millions and at the last census had only 4,000.000 (Shame). They had all to deplore the fact that Ireland was a decaying country. (Hear, heir.) They were told that they had nothing to fear in England but he was afraid that we had something to fear in that direction. The birth rate in England was declining. Last quarter was the lowest on record. He had no panacea for that but we could do something in this matter by considerably diminishing our death-rate. (Hear, hear.) We had been fairly successful in that direction but there was still much to be dune. In regard to

INFANTILE MORTALITY in spite of the march of civilisation and of scientific research, we had to deplore the fact that there were 186 out of every 1,000 children who died before they reached the ace of 12 months. The Act was calculated to do something in that direction, by the maternity benefit cleuse, which provided that the wife Of an insured person received 80s. in four weekly payments of is. Gd. She would get 30s. or Its equivalent. There were some people who took objection to the term "cash or in kind' thinking that the payment ought to be in hard cash. There would be many men out of the 10,000,000 they were going to bring under the Act who could not be trusted with the 30s. They could not be relied upon to pass a public house although their wives

div.head: ALTRINCHAM DIVISION.
div.p: THE ALTRINCHAM DIVISION.
Sir A. Haworth Suggested as a Liberal Candidate.

Rumours are in circulation in the Altrincham division that Mr. J. 11. Kebty-Fletcher, M.P., is about to retire from Parliament on account of his continued ill-health. The leaders of the Conservative patty in the constituency have not, howirter, had any sign of such an intention on the member's pat. Since the end of last session Mr. Fletcher has been unable to fulfil any public engagements, and for a long time past he has been staying at Mundesley-on-Sea, Norfolk, in the expectation of benefitting by the climate. From time to time, at meetings in the Altrincham division letters from Mr. Fletcher have been read expressing a hope that he might shortly be able to resume his Parliamentary duties. A week ago the officials of the Conservative organisation heard that the member's health was improving. It is known that for some time he has conducted his own correspmdence. Early in the year, when the possibility of a by- electi n seemed far from remote, the Liberals of the division appointed a committee to consider the position, and, with the full approval of the Chief Whip, a candidate was chosen. In the circumstances it was deemed advisable to withhold his name from publication. When the meeting of the Association was held last month the action of the committee was confirmed, though at the same time the chairman said if there was no contest till the general election the matter might be reconsidered. Since then Sir Arthur Haworth has been spoken of as a possible candidate, and it is thought that he may be invited to stat.d. Sir Arthur is well known in the division, where he lives and where he was for a con- siderable time an office-holder in the Liberal Association.

div.head: JEWS FINED FOR GAMING.
div.p: JEWS FINED FOR GAMING.

Twentv-three Jews who were concerned in the recent raid by the police on a gaming house at Rugby-street, Cbeetham, were tined at Manchester City Police Court, on Wednesday, but the magistrates stated that they could not grant an application that the two principal defendants, the occupier of the house and her husband, should be recommended for deportation.

LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
NATIONALIZATION OF MINES APPROVED.
Socialists' Novel Proposal.

In view of the deadlock in the coal industry, the debate on the proposed socialisation of the mines at the meeting of the Warrington Parliamentary Debating Society on Tuesday evening, had a special interest. There was a large attendance of Socialists in the public gallery and the various sections of the House were also well represented. Mr C DUKES (Socialist, West Ham) introduced the following resolution : "That this House realizing the grave effects upon the community of the present crisis in the coal trade recommends the immediate socialisation of the mines as the only effective way of establishing industrial peace in tire coalfields and assuring the miner of a living wage. The approximate value of the mines being .£120,000,000 this House recom- mends the issue of bonds for this amount carrying interest at three per cent, per annum ; that a sum of £3,000,000 he set aside annually for the purpose of paying off the debt, thus leaving approximately £9,500,000 to be used for the purpose of bettering the conditions of the misers and reducing the price of coal to the community." He pointed out that there were something like 1,000,000 men and boys in the coal industry highly organized with the definite object of obtaining trot a mimumum but a maximum wage—that was to say, they had organized for the one purpose of salting wages to the highest possible level. On the other hand they had the Employers Federation organized with the sole object of exacting the utmost farthing in, pie fits. (" No.") He said disticctly " Yes." As a consecrience it was utterly impossible to draft sny Bill, short of the socialisatien of the Mines, that would restore perpetual peace between the two conflicting interests. One party was fighting for the monopoly of his lebour power, while the other Was fighting for a monopoly of markets, or rather of the commodity he produced. The °eller must therefore of recessity alwsos attempt to drive labour p rwer down to its lovi est level, with the otject of keeping out of the market any competition, foreign or otherwise, that might be brought to Lea . The miner was organised to negative the coal- owner's attempts in that direction. Was the nation to stand by, awaiting the final outcome of the coi flint, or was it to make the mineral wealth of the coal fields national property, to he worked in the interests of the community as a whole instead of, as at present, in the interests of a few cal owners who in times of panic raised prices and took advantage of every hitch in the market ? Every time the miner had attempted to deal with the grievance of abnormal places in a sectional way, he had been defeated. Consequently he was driven to the con- clusion that nothing short of the total paralysis of the industry would achieve his object. Having shown how the application/ of machinery to coal mining had displaced skilled labour,the speaker said we had reached a point at which we had to choose between the trusti- lication of the coal mining industry and its socializa• tion. It was an utter impossibility, according to the simplest law of political economy, to frame a Bill stipulating a fixed minimum. Wages were nominal, real and relative and when it was borne in mind that the purchasing power of the sovereign had decreased something like 10 per cent, in ten yesrs, it was ridicu- lous to suggest that the worker should work a given length of time for a given amount. The suggestion that the minimum wage should be fixed by boards in each district implied a constant conflict. Would the miner be fool enough to ref use to uss his national organization and allow the fight to continua on a sectional basis ? Advocating socialisation, as distinct from nationalisa- tion, the speaker said the time had arrived when we should have industrial democracy instead of bureaucracy. The Post 011;ce was dominated and engineered by men who viewed everything through capitalist spectacles and wished to exact front the community the largest possible profit in order that they might relieve the taxation of the class to which they belonged. The miners were beginning to learn the futility of nationalisation as advocated by Radicals and Labour men generally. They had no more to expect from the State as the State than from the private employer. They were out to fight for social ownership and not State ownership. They did not wish administration by professional politicians. They believed that the Miners' Federation—men who had proved their ability in the field of profs ssionaliam— were the best fitted to carry out in the interests of the whole of the csnimunity the administration of that industry upon which depended all other industries. (Applause) Mr. CHAMBERLAIN (Soc., Gorton), seconded. He expressed regret that the Member for Truro (Rev. E. C. E. Carleton) who made a spscial effort to attend when Welsh Disestab I ishment was under dis- cussion had not seen his way to attend when such an important industrial question war brought forward and that members of the Liberal party, who put in an appearance to deal with the licensing question, were also absent. If society did not settle the industrial question, it would settle society. The need for the socialisation of the mines could not have been more clearly demonstrated than during the present. crisis. They had seen the Liberal pert/ trying to bring forward methods of conciliation and nrbitratioo,and the Tory party was practically silent How was it that the Tories had not used their influence and brought pressure to bear upon the Liberal party to force their hands in effecting a settlement ? The only effective way of dealing eith the question was to take the mines out of the control of the privileged few who worked them for the profits they could exploit out of the miners, and piece them in the hands of the Miners' Federation, to be worked in the interests of the State. Syndicalism was the only means whereby the emancipa- tion of the workers could be brousht about. ltdr L. WaneuiteoN (C., W Bristol), In moving the rejection of the resolution, said public opinion was with the miners in the present dispute. Personally he believed that all places in mines were abnormal—the very fact that a man was down a mine was abnormal. (Hear, hear.) To suggest, however, that the trouble would be settled by the immediate socialization of the mines was ridiculous. How could the Miner's Federa- tion rule prices in the best interests of the community and at the same time give the best possible wage to the miner ? The two things were incon- sistent. The Miners' Federation could not even rule their own men—three-fourths of the miners in the Potteries did not belong to it—and he was afraid no power en earth would force a man to work if he did not wish to. The suggested 3 per cent, would be a good thing for one or two collieries in Scotland, where E t shares could he bought for 4.1,d. flow would the socialization of mines effect great concerns like Pearson ' and Knowles which depended upon coal for the produc- tion of their iron ? It seemed to him that if they , socialized the mines, they must eventually socialise the iron industry and everything else. (Hear. hear.) Before they suggested such a drastic proposal they should show how it could be done. The result of the Socialists' scheme would be that the consumer would have to pay a great deal more for his coal. Mr .1 A Hey woon(L, Limehouse) said the Socialists had a good deal of right on their side but he did not see why they should object to nationalisation of the mines. In his opinicn that plan would meet the demands of the workers quite as well as socialisation. He intended to wait and see what course the debate took, ,efore committing himself to vote either way. Mr E ENGLAND (1., Warrington) : Wait and see which way the cat jumps. Mr HEY WOOD : Not quite that. I generally have fixed convictions. lam not like some other members of the House. (Much laughter). Mr ENGLAND: Wise men move with the times. (Laughter). Mr Hey WOOD : Yes and they come back again. (Laughter). Continuing he commented upon the apathy of the Opposition in the present crisis and said that judging from the Tory Press, they bad been against the miners all through—as they were always against anything for the benefit of the workers. The Home SECRETARY (Mr M Howarth) raid most of them were in fay Cr of the nationalisation of certain industries, but when they were told that the whole management of a complex business with international relations was to be placed in the hands of the miners who—he thought he could say without disrespect—had no commercial knowledge, it was calculated to make one thinks little bit. (Hear, hear.) Ile was quite pre pared to support the nationalisation of miners although he did not agree that it was the only effective way of meeting the present difficulty. Some scheme of com- pulsory arbitration would settle the trouble quite as adequately as nationalisation. (A VOICE: " And the Government.") He did not support the- resolution primarily for its effect on labour and wages. Sir William Ramsay,in an address to the British Association gave a very emphatic warning against the great danger to our industries of the diminution of the coal supply. Ile calculated that if the present accelerated increase in output were continued, at the end of 175 years the coal pits of this country would be exhausted. There was no greater menace facing our industries and no greater national crime than the manner in which this precious product Was being wasted. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: SWINTON V. RUNCORN: LINNETS FAIL TO SCORE.
div.p: SWINTON V. RUNCORN: LINNETS FAIL TO SCORE.

The meeting of these teams in their rettun engage- ment at Chorley-road attracted a crowd of 4,000 people, and a well-contested game was witnessed. Swinton were much more polished in finishing off their attacks than the" Linnets," and they deservedly wcn. The first half saw Swinton pressing almost con- tinuously, but the visitors put up a strong defence,and it was nearing the interval when Bailey, receiving from Wharton, dashed over in a good position, for Ryder to kick a goal. Runcorn were thus five points in arrears when the half-time whistle sounded. In the second half Swinton soon improved their position with an uncon- verted try by Morris,whilst close on time a clever piece of play by Dai Davies enabled Fairhurst to crosg again, Morris ;Jailing to improve. Result :—Swinton I goal, and 3 tries (11 points), Runcorn nil.
WIDNES V. EBBW VALE.

Played at Widnes, before 4,C00 spectators. The visitors were the first to score, Jenkins placing a goal after Widnes bad been penalised for obstruction. The home backs showed some excellent combination, and Laws ran in two very flue tries after good work by Dainteth. Jones improved one of them, and at half- time Widnes led by 8 points to 2. The second half was very much in favour of Widnes, and it was seldom that the visitors got out of their own half. O'Gara crossed after a fine individual effort,and Swinton scored at the corner by means of a passing movement. Jenkins kicked a penalty goal for Ebbw Vale. Result :—Widnes I goal 4 tries (14 points) ; Ebbw Vale,2 goals (4 points). ST. HELENS v. SALFORD.—" SAINTS" RETAIN [FOURTH POSITION.

There teams met for the third time this season before 5,000 spectators at St Helens. St Helens attacked through Browning and Greenwood, the latter handing to slolyneux, who scored. Shallcross failed. Salford could not get out of their half, and Flanagan made a final effort, but being foiled he dropped at goal, the leather striking one of the uprights, and Shallcross rush- ing up scored in a Salford mix-up. Turtill easily improved. Salford changed the aspect of affairs, and from pressure close in, Turtill missed his kirk and Pugsley scored, Mesley failing. Resuming, Trenwith dribbled away from the centre, and beating Launce and Mesley scored, Molyneux kicking a good goal. Green- wood, from a round of passing scored at the corner, Shallcross just failing, and from clever combination Molyoeux again'got over, Turtill failing. In the last minute of the game Salford passed on the home line, and Rees scored, but Mesley failed to augment. Result: —St Helens, 2 goals, 5 tries (19 points) ; Salford, 2 tries (G points).

div.head: LANCASHIRE SHIELD. RUNCORN "A" V. ROCHDALE "A."
div.p: LANCASHIRE SHIELD. RUNCORN "A" V. ROCHDALE "A."

These teams met on the Incell-lane ground on Satur- day to decide the semi-final for the Lancashire Shield. The Runcorn team included a fair number of first team men viz : Bate ; J W lloaworth, Moran, Hughes and Abel ; Jos. Hoxworth and Lewis ; Massey, Jones, Inman, Prince, Kirkham and S Walker. In the first half the Linnets had all the play and put on 13 points. Rochdale improved later, but were beaten by 13-8. The other semi-final between Millom and Barrow was drawn, (; points each.

div.head: FRIENDLY MATCH.
div.p: FRIENDLY MATCH.

WAftnISGToN "A " V FLIXTON.—These teams met at Wilderspool before a good crowd. Warrington had Daintith and Brooks at half back, but the visitors were the first to get on the offensive and Riley put the finish on some good work with a smart try. Warring- ton were not long in equalising, as Jolley took a pass from Brooks, and cut through the defence cleverly, for Povey to plant the ball over the line. Jolley kicked a goal. Half-time, Warrington 5 points, Flixton 3 points In the second half Warrington had matters pretty much their own way, though they were beaten forward. Jolley was again prominent, and Brooks rushed over near the posts, Jolley converting. Shortly after Brooks felt the effects of an old injury and retired. Daintith and Jolley again led the attack, and Clare scored at the corner, Jolley kicking a third fine goal. Before the close Cooper scored after loose forward I play and a weak kick by Cochrane. No goal followed. I Final : Warrington " A 3 goals, 4 tries, 18 points; Flixton, 1 try, 3 points.

div.head: IMPROBABILITY OF WAR IN EUROPE.
div.p: THE IMPROBABILITY OF WAR IN EUROPE.

" War between European nations, because of their interdependence and because of their interlacing of national life, becomes every day more difficult and improbable." This was the conclusion reached by Lord Esher in thocourEe of an address before the members of the Royal United Service Institution on Wednesday on The co-ordination of naval and military defences." "it seems to roe almost unthinkable," Lord Esher declared, " that Great Britain or Germany or FraLce should ever again in cold blood let loose upon each other the forces of war." Just as wars on the Continent of Europe lasting thirty or even seven years had become impossible, so war of any kind in the same sphere tended to become more difficult and improbable.

div.p: ALTRINCHAM LADS Vc.. LATCHFORD.

This game took place on Stamford Park before a fair attendance, and vc as of a very close nature all throuoa, for a long time neither side claiming any advantage. In the end Latabford just about deserved their victory with the score : Latchford, two goals ; Altrincham Lads, one. LOSIOCK GI:ALAN V OUGHTRINGTON PARK.

At Lostock. Oughtrington Park were the visitors at Lostock and could only muster ten men, consequently they were overplayed all through and msiuly on the defensive. For a long time Simpson and his backs fought manfully against some splendid combination by the home attack. lot in the end had to admit defeat with the score :—Lostock Gralam, five ; Oughtrington Park, nil. lOUGIITRINGTON AMATEURS V ST. _CROSS.

At Heatley. To enable St. Cross to fulfil another engagement at Lymm, an early kick-aff took place. St. Cross opened well and for a time play was even. Settling down the Amateurs took a firmer hold of th 3 game, gradually gaining the upper hand, winning easily before the close by four goals to nil. •

div.head: LYMM V. ST. CROSS.
div.p: LYMM V. ST. CROSS.

At Lymm. At the commencement St. Cross were first away and had by far the best of the game. They were the first to score through Whalley. This reverse aroused Lymm, who tried hard to grt, on even terms. After some good work Owen equalized. Once spin level, Lymm had the best of the argument, and scoring three times quickly led at the interval by four goals tti one. In the second half, as one would naturally expect, St. Cross tired and the game was entirely in favour of Lymm, who eventually ran out easy winners by eight goals to one. For Lymm: Webb three, Owen two, Whitfield, Dunn, and Potter were the scorers.

Lyrom Lads were the first to open the score, Barber finding the net with a good effort. Jho game still ruled even, and before the interval Latchford deservedly equalized. Half-time, one goal erch. In tle second half play was again of a very even nature and with each side scoring an additional goal, the game resulted in a draw of two goals each.

div.head: "TERRIBLE RESPECTABILITY."
div.p: "TERRIBLE RESPECTABILITY."
WHY THE CLERK HAS HELD ALOOF FROM TRADE UNIONISM.
INTERESTING MEETING AT WARRINGTON.
"The average life of the average clerk is one long drawn-out tragedy." "Some clerks have to imitate a Duke cn an imitation dustman's wages." . _ _

Such were the declarations of two of the princi?al speakers at a public meeting held in the Co-operative Halt, Sankey-street, on Saturday evening under the joint auspices of the National Union of Clerks and the Itailway Clerks' Association. There was a good attendance presided over by Mr. James Ball. Amongst those on the platform were : The Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph), Messrs. l'eter Peacock, F Wroe (vice-president J Hazelip (general treasurer N.U.C.), J St. Clair Halfpenny (official organiser 11.C.A.), Hiscocks (Manchester), C W Blanchard (Liverpool) and Fitzpatrick. Mr. Harold Smith, M.P., was billed to speak, but wrote regretting his inability to be present. " In the beginning of my business life " he wrote " I worked under conditi ns which often crushed my enthusiasm and injured my health. I have never departed from the views which were then forced upon me, that there is much to be done in the alleviation of the hard lot of the clerk. From inquiries I have made I am satis- fied that the bard conditions that, prevail in most of our big cities are scarcely to be found in Warrington. Much can be done by organization on strictly non- political lines, and I commend the object of your association to the clerks of Warrington. " Mr A. 11. Crosfield, who is abroad, conveyed his sincere good wishes for the prosperity of the Union, and expressed the hope that the meeting would be a very successful one. Lord Woluaer, M.P., and Councillor Ef. Roberts also sent letters of apology. The CHAIRMAN said that in these days of complex industry it was almost impossible for any class of employment to allow itself to be dealt with individually. For many reasons the combination and association of all sorts of professions and employments had become one of the most marked features of latter day life. He could not understand why the clerks as a body should have stayed outside trade unionism so long. After all, the clerk had only his labour, experience and know- ledge to sell, like any workman, labourer or artizan in tbe works round about him. Under the stress of modem competition it had become absolutely essential that there should be organised bodies on both sides and he urged the clerks to combine for their own protection and advancement. (Applause). Mr. J. ST. CL.A.IR HALFPENNY said the minimum wage for a railway clerk or for any clerk in the provinces was £3 a week—that was the minimum below which he could not exist in the business sense. Just as a business man

Many clerks, although they were living within the radius of respectability, received little more than the unskilled labourer. Labour of all kinds was dignified, even if it were unskilled, but he failed to see the dignity of a skilled labour which bad to live in such a manner that a person could not pty his way. (Hear, hear). Ills worship suggested that there should be a

PRELIMINARY EXAMINATION with the object of restricting the number of persons entering the clerical profession. At the present time many people went in for clerkships because they did not like manual labour, whereas some of them might be better fitted for really good work pf a manual kind. There was one matter in which he did not quite sympathise with NI r. izalip—he did not hope that the clerk would be able rather in the near or distant future to cause the same amount of disturbance that was threaten- ing us through the coal strike which struck at the life and trade of the country and was a teal calamity. Although he had sympathy with the clerks or with any- body else who had grievances, being united and strong in their determination to gain their just rights in a proper manner, he had no sympathy with anything that STRICR AT THE LIFE, II E A LTII AND TRADE OF TIIE

CJUNTRY in the manner that the coal strike was doing. (Applause). Mr. F. Witog, in seconding, said they all deplored such a national calamity as the miners had been com- pelled to bring abou', but was not the life of the clerk and of the miner a calamity for which the nation must ba held responsible ? (Hear, hear.) Unless they were enabled to strike at the heart of society, society would never recognise them. Therefore, whether they would or not, they were bound at times to take the bull by the horns and state their terms in the most uncom- promising fashion possible. The average life of the average olerk was a long drawn out tragedy. They ould do nothing by sitting down and hoping for better conditions. No great reform was ever gained without great sacrifice. Mr. P. PEACOCK supported. He said that owing to modern educatisnal advantages the clmrnercial world was flooded with would-be clerks. Was the average wage for clear; in Warrington 25s a week ? He said emphatically " No." The average in Warrington did not compare at all with that of the dock labourers and the ordinary labourers who were organized. ("Shame.") Yet they had to dress respectably and go to work almost as if they were " bosses." (Laughter). As one who had been through the mill, he asked them in all eatnestmess to join the Union, especially in view of the Insurance Act. Be pointed out that it would be impossible for the employer to tell, by looking at the I insurance card, that the clerk belonged to a trade union. Referring to the other grievances of the clerks, Mr. Peacock said that in many instances it was impossible to obtain promotion by merit alone; they must have influence. Directors' sons, nephews, relations and friends were put into good positions and the clerks had to teach them their work before they were competent. He believed trade unionism would help to remove those inequalities. With regard to the suggested examinations, did clerks went to be examined to start atss. or tis.a week and get 2s.a week advance at the end of the year? The first thing to do was to get properly organized,and make the clerks' calling a real profession on a par with other highly organized bodies. They would be satisfied with less than a a week as a minimum. When some- thing like a decent wage had been obtained they could say We don't want any rotters in our Union ; we want only the men who are worthy of more than they are getting." The employer would then share in the advantages by having a superior staff. (Applause.) The resolution was unanimously agreed to. Mr. HISCOCKS proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman and speakers. Mr. BLANCHARD in seconding, said the clerk some- times had to imitate a Duke on an imitation dustman's wages. (Laughter). The vote was heartily carried.

div.head: BOWLING.
div.p: BOWLING.
WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIATiON. PETER PEAC.:OCI): CHALLENGE CUP.

A competition on the" knock-out" system has been arranged from the coming season, among the Wards in town. Mr. Peter Peacock has very generously pus- chased the cup which is on view at the Liberal Club, Bewsey-street. Medals will be provided for the winners and runners up. The teams will consist of 12 and wards may enter as many teams as they wish. The officers are desirous that all shall take part in the games whether able to play the game or not, and the following rule to enable this to be done has been framed accordingly :—A Ward having more than 12 entries, the first 12 drawn out of the hat shall comprise one team;the second 12 another team, and so on, and if a number not sufficient to comprise a full team be left in the hat, then these shalt form a reserve to be called upon to fill vacancies in their ward teams. The Wards ate being called together as quickly as possible, and entries are coming in rapidly. The day for closing the entries is Saturday April 13th, and an invitation is heartily given to all those Liberals willing to assist and work for Liberalism, to joie the Wards, and take part in the competition. The entrance fee is Is. and this will include admission to take part in a grand bowling main at the conclusion of the competition. Mr. William Campbell, the proprietor of the Bowling Green Inn, has very generously placed his green at the disposal of the committee for the season, so that there ' is every prospect of a very enjoyable season for all Liberal workers.

The following officers and Committee have been appointed to carry the competition and main through the season :—Chairman, Councillor J Wilkinson, J.P. ; deputy chairman, Mr Hlford ; hon. treasurer, Mr G T Rushton ; hon. secretary, Mr Ernest A Sanders ; committee, Town Hall, Mr W Taylor ; Whitecross, Mr J Dutton ; Bewsey No. 3, Mr J Waring ; Be-csey No. 4 Mr J Coyne ; Orford, Mr G Millington ; St. John's No. 6, Mr W Alcock ; St. John's No. 7.Nlr E G Hughes; Fairfield, Mr S H Walker ; Howley, Mr M Llewellyn ; St. Austin's No. 10, Mr J Wilkes ; St. Austin's No. 11. Mr E J Davies ; Latchford No. 12, Mr .1 Mather ; Latchford No. 13, Mr J Walker ; Orford Village, Mr P H Brown. The reserves attached to the winning teams shall play in the second round.

dare not sell his articles below coßt price without becoming bankrupt, so the clerk could not sell his labour below £3 a week without becoming bankrupt. As a matter of fact, however, railway cleiks and other clerks were bankrupt to-day. The only way for a clerk to be able to replace himzelf when be was superannuated or thrown on the scrap heap, was by having sufficient family, so that when he retired his sons might take his place. The minimum salary of a clerk must be such a figure as would enable him to keep a family of three at least, and in Warrington that took £3 week. The speaker showed how the amount was arrived at by making allowances for rent (Bs. per week, for house with bath), food, clothing, medical attendance, annual holiday of a fortnight,nlawspapers, o. The railway directors, he continued, had been very quick in granting the principle. What the clerks could not get u,as the hard cash. It was absolutely immoral for railway directors or anybody else to talk about principles by themselves. A -principle could no more exist apart from the price than the body could apart from the soul. Some of the talk of the past few weeks about the principle of things had been absolutely dis- gusting. The clerks were going to get the figure for which they mere contending. They intended to keep up the pre,sure not only by better organisation but by using every legitimate weapon in their hands. Not the last of those weapons was the Parliamentary as distinct from the political weapon and the rgrlway clerk had already found it very useful. If commercial clerks would make use of it they would be able to obtain not the principle but the substance. (Applause). Mr. J. 11A7ELIP said the great stumbling block in connection with trade unionism for clerks had always been •

THE TERRIBLE RESPECTABILITY or THE CLERK. If 20,000 or 30,000 medical men could combine for the purpose of maintaining a living wage, it ought to be patent to every clerk that young men whose minimum wage was not 30s a week should follow in the footsteps of the medical profession and endeavour to get a living wage for themselves by organization and combination. (Applause). In accountancy, the legal profession, the army and navy and the civil service they found close associations working to maintain the status of their members. This was the dry of com- binations. The tendency of the time was for affairs of industry and State to be carried on in a whole- sale style. They had to recognize that the day of individual bargaining between employer and employed was passed, and if the clerks desired better, conditions they would have to do what all the manual and artizati workers had done—send in their requests as a combined body, and they would be certain of receiving respectful attention. The National Union of Clerks had become an approved s iciety and would take advantage of the Insurance Act, wherever it was possib'e to do so. They% were a trade union and, incidentally, a friendly society, but their chief aim and object was to raise the status of the clerk as a wage earner, and not merely to make provision for him when he ' happened to be ill. By becoming a Post Office contributor, a clerk would get very little but by joining the Union of Clerks he could either take the section which gave the State benefits only, or join the various sections and make provision for all the vicissi- tudes to which one was subject in the clerical profession. Mr. Hazelip showed how the Union had succeeded in getting clerks placed under the fair contracts clauses of various public bodies and they had also been instrumental in securing an addition of £ll,OOO to the wages of clerks employed by the Port of London Authority. (Applause.) The Union was affiliated with the Labour Party and he claimed that during the past few years they bad received a good return from that affiliation. (Applause.) We were living in a period of unrest, and he would die happy if he lived to see the day whsu the National Union of Clerks could

MAKE SUCH A STIR IN THE LAND AS THE MINERS were making at the present. (Applause). The MAYOR moved a resolution pledging the meeting to support the Warrington branches of the National Union of Clerks and the Railway Clerks' Association in their efforts to organize the local clerks and thus make the branches strong and powerful. he emphasised the tact that union is strength. If the clerks were united and joined a Union, they bad power to make certain terms for themselves and also to draw up definite rules for their own improvement. They could broaden their education in their own particular line of work and thus make themselves more valuable to their own employers and a greater power with the community of employers. Too much importance could not be attached to that aspect of the case. In his own profession, if the mcdical men of the present day \Vete not as a rule highly skilled and educated in their work, they would not have had the same power with the Chancellor of the Exchequer and those who were carrying out the , details of the Insurance Act as they evidently had had. div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
"The Executioner's Daughter."

The drama loving public of Warringtcn have been well catered for of late by the management of the Royal Court Theatre. For some weeks past the " boat ds" of this popular place of entertainment have been occupied by strong companies in exceptionally lurid productions, and the fare provided this week is no c xception to the rule. 'The Executioneer's daughter "is a production full of awe-inspiring and hair-raising incidents which are well pourtrayed. The scenic effects are of the best arid the staging of the production is perfect. The story is well told, and deals with the "heart troubles " of Paul novel and the executioners's daughter in a clever and intricate manner. Of course there is the inevitable intervention of villainous schemes ably carried out by the artistes who have the interpretation of these unsavoury parts in hand. Mr. P. W. Mansfield as Felix Marius, the head of the unscrupulous gang of thieves and gamblers, gives a fairly good interpreta- tion of the part, although his style is rather lacking in finish. Nevertheless the audience seem to overlook this fact and his cffovs are rewarded with a large amount of complimentary hisses and boos. Mr. Stanley Radcliffe, as Mons. Roche, the public execu- tioner played the part with exceptional ease, and his acting especially in the act where he was called upon to execute his own daughter was loudly applauded. Miss Beatrice Malvern as Annetta, the executioner's daughter, soon earns the sympathy and appreciation of the audience for her able portrayal of the girl who was wrongly doomed to the guillotine and who was eventually rescued by her lover Mr. J. Leon Courtville, as Paul Rovel. He is an actor who puts all his energy in the part and at once is a favourite with the audience. Miss Amy Ellam is an able accomplice to Marius and equally shares the reward of merit. Mr. Lancelot Usher and Miss Cissy Cleveland keep the house in an uproar with their absurdities and humorous acting. Their efforts are successful in maintaining throughout the play a supply of humour which somewhat enlightens the heavier aspects of the production. Miss Agnes Jesmond plays the part of the cripple in a clever manner and at once arouses the sympathetic instincts of the audience. Mr. Fred A. Marston as Kretch, the useful tool in the hands of Marius, also gives a skilful presentment of the heavy ritle. NEXT WEEK. "THE WITNESS FOR THE DEFENCE."

Lovers of the dramatic art, artistically presented, should not fdit to pay a visit to the Court Theatre next week when Mr. Alban B. Limpus company will appear in the famous play "The witness for the defence." The play is by Mr. [A. E. W. Mason, the famous novelist and playwright, and had a successful run in London at the St. James' Theatre with Sir George Alexauder in the title role. It is a play that will appeal to all those who can enjoy a piece bristling with genuine human interest, abounding in mysteries and thrills of expectation. It grips you from the rise of the curtain, and there is an enthralling atmos- phere which produces a most fascinating influence on the audience.

div.head: " KISMET " AT THE SHAKESPEARE THEATRE, LIVERPOOL.
div.p: " KISMET " AT THE SHAKESPEARE THEATRE, LIVERPOOL.

The visit of " Kismet," the wonderfully fascinating Arabian night's tale, to the Shakespeare, Liverpool, next week, is creating considerable interest,and already the bookings point to crowded audiences throughout the stay. Originally written in German, the play has an interesting history. It was refused by every theatrical manager in Berlin as unsuitable for the stage. Mr. Edward Knoblauch, the author' who is a cosmopolitan scholar, then translated it into French, and approached a number of Parisian managers, but the play was again rejected, Mr. Knoblauch, however, set to work, and re-wrote the play in English, and submitted it to the whole of the managers in New York, but still theatrical managers would have nothing to do with the produc- tion. Mr. Knoblauch then tried several London managers, and again he met with disappointment. As a last resource he sent his manuscript to Mr. Oscar Asche, who accepted and produced the play within two months. The play was an instantaneous success, and it continues to draw crowded audiences wherever it, is produced. I Liverpool may congratulate itself on having secured a visit of one of the most talked-of plays in the United Kingdom. " Kismet " was perhaps the most interest- ing theatrical production of 1911, and has played to figures that seem likes fairy tale, over £155,000, since April 19th last. Many who have not seen " Kismet are inquiring what it is. " Kismet is is drama, but a drama of such a select and sweet kind that it is difficult to liken it to anything produced in the past. In the first place it is Oriental, absolutely, in its con- ception and staging, and the Orient, with its vivid :colouring, lends itself excellently to stage pictures. " Kismet " is an Eastern story of l atred, bloodshed, love and revenge. Its centre character is a beggar— Gajj—who murders with a joke upon his lips and a smile upon his face. It is produced in an Eastern atmosphere) with all the gorgeous settings and effects. The harem scece, the bath scerm and the mosque scene are veritable transportations of the East to the West. Studying local colc,ur in Tunis, the author has grasped all the de ails as well as the main points which show the life of the Eastern potentate, the Eastern woman, the dancing girl, the snake charmer, the juggler and the beggar. "Kismet " is bound to meet with an enthusiastic reception. Mr. George Dance has made strenuous endeavours to give Liverpool an equal representation to that whirl!' named so high a reputation in London and 1 America.

Who is the Tory- leader? No sooner does Mr. Balfour return to the Commons than Mr. Bonar Law is deposed and the duty of moving the official amendment to the Coal Mines Bill is placed in the hands of his predecessor. * * * _ _

Mr. P. M. Oliver is quickly establishing himself a favourite in the Knutsford Division —and in Warrington too. His trenchant criticisms, straightforward avowal of political beliefs, and the wit which sparkles from every paragraph of his speeches, are circum- stances which combine to secure him ready listeners wherever he goes. He bids fair to shake the Tory stronghold of Knutsford to its foundations in a manner reminiscent of the 1906 upheaval of the villages.

* * * Much of the trouble round Collins Green might have been avoided if one or two owners had not been awkward, and refused to let the miners forage on the tip banks. As showing the honesty and dignity of the men in the crisis, no less a sum than £lOO was on Thursday collected from slot meters in the district, and in no single case had a meter been broken into, though want was acute fn many homes. * *

As we expected, the Protectionist press has been fitting the recent speech of Mr. D. A. Thomas into their patchwork to suit its crazy design. When Mr. D. A. Thomas said that "as far as Ebbw Vale is concerned a little Protection would be a good thing," he added, "I have not, however, yet had it proved that it would be a good thing for the country." The Tariff Reform newspapers do not quote the second sentence. It gives the game away.

f.s • It was a disappointment to Warrington- ians to learn in mid-week that the visit of Miss Marie Corelli to lecture on "The Spirit of Shakespeare" in Parr Hall last evening, had been indefinitely postponed. Owing to the disorganised railway service, and with the possibilities of a decreased attendance as a result of the strike in view, Miss Corelli suggested a postponement which the officers of the "Lit and Phil" had perforce to agree to.

Mr. Harold Smith, M.P., and Lord Wolmer M.P., both voted against the Minimum Wage Bill—a course of action for which we hope their constituents will exs.ct either an adequate explanation or a penalty. Both these gentlemen profess to have the interests of the workers at heart, but when the first Bill for establishing a minimum wage by law in the most dangerous of trades is before the House, they are both found to be slaves of the Opposition. Mr. Harmood Banner, M.P., showed a clearer sense of the fitness of things, and of his duty to the mining com- munity, by voting for the Bill and against his party! •* * •

Mr. Balfour took the reins of leadership from the nerveless hand of Mr. Bonar Law on Thursday, but he made a very poor case against the Government Bill for the settle- ment of the coal strike. His speech reveals Toryism as absolutely bankrupt of any even plausible remedy for the present calamity, and it was pernicious nonsense on his part to say that the miners were devoid of "policy and mercy" their cruelty exceeded that of "feudal barons," their exactions were harsher than that of " the village money- lender" or "the American trust." This is a true Tory attitude towards labour as a whole, which should be remembered against the speaker, and against all those who supported him by their futile votes in the division lobby. • There was a striking incident in the House of Commons on Wednesday. The Tories cheered and cheered again at the news that Tom Mann had been arrested for making seditious speeches. Their jubilation was, however, turned to comical dismay when Mr. Lansbury rose and asked one of those deadly questions which will ring through industrial England." "Why," askei Mr. Lansbury, "has Torn Mann been arrested for inciting to disorder and no proceedings been taken against Privy Councillors for Ireland." This is a pertinent rejoinder to the" Ulster will fight" utterances of Sir Edward Carson, and it completely silenced the Tories. Even the Attorney-General had no answer ready and the Labour Party is entitled to presume that there is one law for them and anothel for " Privy Councillors."

div.head: WINDING UP LADY GREENALL AND HER CLOCKS.
div.p: WINDING UP LADY GREENALL AND HER CLOCKS.
Some Facts About the Trade.

Lady Greenall has found a new champion, but most unfortunately he resembles the clocks in being a "foreigner "—or a specimen of (politically) dumped goods. Mr. England uses our Tariff Reform contemporary to speak of our criticism of Lady Greenall as "an attempt to belitlle a commendable action on her part." Presumably he means that it was commendable at a Dumping Exhibition to give foreign clocks as prizes. We have no desire to belittle any commend- able action, or to treat Lady Greenall in any way unfairly ; all we say is that her action was not consistent with the teachings of the Exhibition. After our first criticism we should have been quite ready to take no further notice of what, after all, was a minor mistake, had not Lady Greenall, instead of franklyadmitting the inconsistency, somewhat rashly defended her action, and attempted to shift the responsibility on to the fiscal system this paper stands to defend. Mr. England, just as rashly, supports her ladyship, repeats her inaccuracies about our losing the watch and clock industry, and states that she gave figures in support of her statement. These figures were misleading and incomplete, because there is no deduction for re-exports, and even if accurate they in no way support her statements.
ONE OF THE CLO:-ES made in Germany) arid preened by Lady Greena: the Dump Exhibition.

We will begin by using the extracts which Mr C. E. Parker, in his remarks at the meeting in Wycliffe School on Monday, gave of the Chairman's speeches at the annual general meeting of a large British clock and watch manufacturing firm—H. Williamson, Limited. February 19th, 1909. " Low priced cloi ks had been almrst entit produced abroad and had hal a laige ale in ti country ; the directors, thetef..re, c.eteimined to construct Engli h clocks of sound a:A reliable quality to compete with such foi sign gocds and had been most successful in so doing. They had met with mot gratifying support in their efforts to revive the watch and clock making industries of this country." July 10th, 1010. " We have found it necessary to make exten- sions and to modernise and enlarge our factory and many of our properties, which have been more than doubled in number during these fifteen years without any increase of the capital of the company. Before I close I should like to point out that when the dividend warrants are posted to-morrow, we shall have returned an amount equal to the whole of the capital of the company, namely, £150,000, to the shaieholders in dividends." 14th Annual Meeting, February 16th, 1912. "The amount of profit earned—iB3,333 (this subject to interests &c.) is the largest on record in the history ef the Cosipany, with one excep- tion, and the volume of trade done during the year far exceeds that of any previous year. This is the most gratifying evidence of ur Company's growing popularity, and of the trade's apprecia- tion of our xuaLufactutes. We are now well equipped in our new factory, and able to produce several important clock lines, which are in con- siderable demand, and we have many valuable contracts booked for the same. The new manage- ment at our Coventry watch factory is giving the utmost satisfaction. The demand for our new Astral English watch and other lines produced at this factory has been such that we have been obliged to largely increase cur output, and upwards of 100 new hands have been added to the factory staff during the year." After this, any further comment on Lady Greenall's statement that our clock and watch industry has been killed is unnecess- sary. The failure of the Prescot Watch Factory has been hinted at in Mr. England's fetter, in which a doleful extract is given from a pamphlet by a Prescot watchmaker. We have no desire to bring into the glare the commercial and financial reasons for the ailure of the Prescot clock and watch venture. But speaking in general terms and sustained by the experience of H. William- son, Limited, we are justified in coming to the conclusion that where business enterprise and sound finance are directed to this trade there is no reason why it should not be eminently successful. And obviously, Lady Greenall could have obtained appropriate prizes in good English made clocks from such firms as H. Williamson, Limited. Lady Greenall, by laying emphasis on three words in her letter, may seek to cover her inconsistency. She says "Owing entirely to the policy of the Free Imports party the English trade in this class ot clock has been killed by the foreign dumper." The necessary interpretation of the words is missing, but the clocks imported into England and including "this class" only •averaged 3s. sd. each. There was no English trade to kill. English; manufacturers, wisely or unwisely, do not consider it worth while to make a 3s. sd. clock, and Lady Greenall was so far right in saying she was compelled to buy " this class" of clocks. She felt she must have a foreign-made clock as a prize for ardent anti-dumpers. But a word or two about the foreigner who, having killed our industry, "flow charges his own price." The average prices of clocks imported during the following years were :- 1899, 6/5 each. 1901, 5/8 each. 1910, 35 each. If the foreigner had killed our industry and eliminated competition why should he charge in 1910 only about half the price of the 1899 imports? He seems to have missed one of the short cuts to becoming a millionaire! Further to show that the home trade is regaining its hold on the home market we give the figures of the imports of clocks, watches, and parts in 1901 and. 1911. Imports 1901 1,960,905. Imports 1011 It would appear the demand for the foreign article is declining, and our people who want accurate timekeepers are buying the products
Decrease
`,IIIA I

of English manufacture; this is specially so in watches. It seems strange it should be left to the Committee of our Dump Exhibi- tion to try and keep up foreign imports by buying and advertising these low priced foreign clocks.

While, as shown, the imports into this ' country are diminishing, the imports into Germany and the United States, (in spite of the increased price to the user as the result of tariffs) are increasing. Thus in this trade recent tendencies demonstrate that the policy of free imports, not for these articles alone, but free imports of everything, is more successful in reducing the imports of watches and clocks than the Protectionist policy of Germany and the United States and the British trade will con- tinue to prosper in spite of the support given to the foreigner by the President of the War- rington Dump Exhibition.

Evelyn-street School. . Over 150 applications have been received for the headmastership of the Evelyn-street Council school. They were brought before the School Management Committee on Thursday and referzed to a special sub- committee for consideration. Church Society Lectures. _ - - -

The Lenten Lectures in connection with the Warr- ington Church Society were :continued yesterday, when in the afternoon the Rev. Bernard. Heywood, vicar of Swinton, delivered an address to women on "Thoughts about our Lord's Incarnation" and in the evening a great number of men listened to his discourse on " Belief in God. Clatworthy, of the Warrington School of Art, for a very complete set of studies of early seals, comprising some of the best types of heraldic examples, very thoroughly studied and well executed. In this work, as should always be the case, a correct and succinct historic statement has been placed under each example. " Warrington Photographic Society.

Through another substitution the members present on Tuesday (about 30) had the pleasure of hearing Mr. W. Tansley of the Everton Camera Club, the hon. secretary of the Lancashire and Cheshire Photographic Union. He, with admirable promptitude, took the place of Mr. T. Lee Sims, F.R P.S., of Leigh, and gave about 89 pictures concerning "The Hundred of Wirral." From New Brighton to Sbotwick, from HoVlake to Brornborough tie lecturer took his audience, giving them interesting details of history and fable, of tradition, of personal recollections. Mr. Tansley was heartily thanked at the close. LAWN MOWERS ground by special machinery. Send your machines now before the rush.—J. S. GARLAND, 51, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt. • The populariy of the concerts promoted by the Warrir gton Epuitable Industrial Co-operative Scciety was stintingly derrions•rab d by the large gathering which assemb'ed tt the last concert of the season which was held in the Co-operative Hall on Thursday evening. The s ciety b s been successful in securing the services of many tahnted artistes throughout the season and the programme on Thursday was ably snsttined by the Northern Operatic Concert Co., one of the smartest compar ies of its kind in the provinces. The programme included several attractive scenas, songs, °nets and choruses rrhich were given with artistic skill and musicianly insight. The entertain- ment wid be a p!easurshle recollection to all who were privileged to hear it. Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds. - • •

The quarterly meeting of members connected with the Late Spring Rose Lolge, No. 828, was held on Saturday, March 16th, at the house of Bro. James Cleave, Barley Mow Hotel. The accounts for the past quarter were submitted by the Secretary, P.M. W. E. Clegg, shoeing that after paying £lO3 for sick benefit a gam of £27 is added to the capital making the total worth of the lodge, i£2,520. After the election of lodge and district officers, P.P.O S. Frederick S. Massey presented to P.M. George Ratcliffe a framed emblem of merit for services rendered to the lodge. P.P.C.S. William Taylor, P.M. William Peers and P.M. James Atkinson added their , testimony to the attentive and good work done by Bro. Ratcliffe during his teim of office. Bro. Ratcliffe suitably responded Master Tailors' and Cutters' Association. The Warrington and District Master Tailors' and Cutters' Association held its annual dinner at the Lion Hotel the other evening, the President, Mr. W. Parry, in the chair. Thee was a good attendance of members and friends from the Warrington and Liver- pool Societies. The toast of " The King. Queen, and the other members of the Royal Family," was given by the Chairman, and that of " The Warriegton and District Master Tailors' and Cutters' Association " by Mr. J. W. Vittles, of Liverpool, and replied to by Mr. J. Poyser. "The Town and Trade of Warrington" was in the hands of Mr. J. Beswick, and Mr. W. H. Walker replied. The toast of " Kindred societies" was proposed by Mr. J. Williams, and Mr. Ireland, of Liverpool, responded. Other toasts were submitted and responded to. A choice programme was pro- vided by Messrs. J. H. Draper, W. N. Ireland, T. It. Ciitchley, T. Healing and A. Nield. Mr. Walter Moores was the accompanist.

Hearts of Oak Society. The sixth annual dinner of the Hearts of Oak Society (Warrington and District Branch), was held at the Winmarleigh Café on Thursday evening and proved an unqualified success. Bro. A. C. Binks presided over a large gathering and submitted the loyal toasts. He also proposed the "Hearts of Oak Society," Bro. W. Kilduff responding. "The doctor" was proposed by Delegate J. T. Rogers and acknowledged by Dr. Law. Bro. Cotterill proposed the health of "The Visitors," Mr. Adams responding. An admirable musical programme was submitted, Mr Bert Smith being an efficient accompanist and also contributing a pianoforte solo. Songs were credit- ably rendered by Mr Walter Moores, Bro. Hatton and Bro, Kilduff. Dr. Law gave recitations and monologues in his usual powerful and effective style and Mr A Wh;te's elever exhibition of conjuring proved plpular. The artistes were thanked on the proposition of Bro. Downing.

The Spiritualist Society. The fifteenth anniversary of this society was celebrated on Sunday. The speaker for the day was Mrs Russell, of Liverpool, who spoke of the work that had been done in that period, and the spiritual benefits many had received, but pressed home to her hearers the question as to how much they had done for Spiritualism. The President also referred to their I commencement as a society, and rejoiced that they still had with them some of the first members, though some were not now taking an active interest in the work. On Monday evening the annual Lyceum tea party and social were held. A goodly number of adults j ined the Lyceurnists at tea, two sittings down being necesaitated. After tea, songs, recitations, &c, were given, and games were entered into with spirit. Twoitems rendered by Mr Gilbert, assisted by eight girls (in character) were especially pleasing. In one the gentleman was got up as a Chinaman and the girls as Japanese ; in the other -(" Here comes the dream man ') the girls were-in night attire, with lighted candles, thus rendering the song very realistic. Big Attraction at the Picturedrome. At the Picturedrome next week the star picture for nday will be "Sister's Love," and for Thursday "Sergeant White's Peril." For the entire week com- mencing April Ist the enterprising proprietors of this p.ipular house have secured the exclusive right for Warrington of the dramatic film " The Lady of the Camellias,' the principal part of which is enacted by Madame Sarah Bernhardt. In this role this world- famed actress has delighted audiences in the regular theatres in all parts of the world, and it certainly marks an epcch in photo playing that the greatest tragedienne of modern times has given her talent for the furtherance of wordless depictions. hitherto she has refused all engagements of this description for dramatic art, but the offer to her of an enormous pay- ment has at last made it possible to bring her famous characterisation within the reach of cll. Picturedrome patrons are advised to come early during that week so that they may be sure of securing good seats. Shilling seats can be reserved at matinees without any booking fees, but the continuous system in vogue during the evening performances makes it impossible to book seats at night.
