-His Honour Judge Stanger,K C., delivered judgment at the Warrington County Court on Thursday in the case in which Samuel Hawkins, an ex-painter and decorator, of 114, Winwiek-road, claimed ten guineas as damages from William Chadwick, 11, Mason-street for fraudulent misrepresentation on the sale of a chipped potato and flied fish busineas for which .9..28 was paid. Mr. Steel was for the plaintiff and Mr. Browne represented the defendant. His Honour said in one sense the case was not a had one,as it was not one where people had been induced to buy an absolutely worthless business. The statements made by the defendant and his wife dating the negotiations for the sale of the business were made widi that degree of recklessness which was sufficient to enable the plaint,ff to recover damages The statements with regard to the profits might not have been made as a beautiful falsehood, but they were sufficient to entitle the plaintiff to damages. However, the defendants were justified in selling the business as one which made a ptofit. He gave judgment for the plaintiff for ;li.B with costs on the original amount claimed.

MOTOR CYCLES.—Agent for "Douglas" & "Premier." New Models now in stock. Trials and all information free.-J. S. GARLAND, 51-55, Bridge at., Warring ton.-Advt A Humane Cattle Killer. Chief Inspector Robinson, of London, gave an interesting demonstration of the efficacy of the R.S.P.C.A. humane killcr at Messrs. Singleton's slaughter-house, Bank-street, on Tuesday afternoon, in the presence of a Dumber of butchers, health and police officials. Although the pole-axe, when used by an expert is regarded as, on the whole, a satisfactory implement, it may, in the hands of a nervous, weak or inexperienced man, be productive of much needless suffering. The R.S.P.C.A. killer is undoubtedly a great improvement on old methods for it is safe, effective and (humane. A fine powerful beast was placed in position, and the spectators had scarcely time to realize what had happened before the whole operation was over. One touch of a spring and a sharp report and the animal was lying lifeless on the floor. There can be no doubt that, all things considered, the bullet is preferable to the axe, for not only is the working of the weapon simplicity itself, but the carcase bleeds quite as freely as if the animal had been pole-axed. We are informed that 1,100 of the killers are now in use. The R.S.P.C.A. has also devised a captive-bolt pistol for stunning small cattle, and a demonstration of its utility was also entirely satisfactory.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH LIBERALS
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH LIBERALS
Mr. P. M. Oliver on Industrial Unrest. THE TORY PARTY IN ITS TRUE COLOURS.

Mr. P. M. Oliver, prospective Liberal candi- date for the Knutsford Division, had an en- thusiastic reception at Stockton Heath on Thursday evening when he addressed a meet- ing in the Providence schoolroom. There ! was a large attendance, Mr. NV. IL,Slierburn ; presiding. There were present on the plat- form : Councillor Roberts, Messrs. Ernest Clarke (Lancashire and Cheshire Liberal Fed- eration), J. Longland, and J. Jarman. The Chairman appealed to young men to take an optimistic view of the present outlook. Although there were so many perplexing problems and the country was in such a state of unrest he did not believe, when matters were viewed in their true perspective, that the British race was degenerating. There never was a period in British history which was so important and full of possibilities as the present time, and it largely depended on the outlook of the present generation .as to whether the lot of those who succeeded us should be brighter or darker. (Applause.) . Mr. Ernest Clarke said Mr. Oliver was mak- ing a name for himself in every part of the division, preparatory, as they hoped, to making a name for himself in the House of Commons. (Applause.) It ought not to be a difficult mat- ter to turn the constituency from its Toryism back to a good Liberal working majority. (Ap- plause.) From whatever point of view they considered politics at the present time, it was absolute folly on the part of any thinking young man to throw in his lot with any other party but the Liberal party. Liberalism had always stood for political rights for the in- dividual, for a juster economic share of things and for the larger prosperity of the whole world. No Government had really got down to the heart of things like the present Adminis- tration. (Applause.) To be on the people's side was not always to.be on the popular side. A fatuous policy, glibly advocated, could gain ascendancy with the people for a time. That was why men like HAROLD SMITH AND TOM MANN

gained the assent of the people for a time, but such tactics only succeeded until the time came when the people found they had been "had." Then came the day of reckoning, and men like Tom Mann and Harold Smith were found out, and the plain, blunt, honest politi- cian came by his own. (Applause.) The treatment of trade unionism and organised working class movements by the Liberal and Tory parties respectively was as different as chalk and cheese. (Applause.) Mr. P. M. Oliver referred to the grave crisis through which the country was passing. The cloud was perhaps darker now than ever it had been, but fortunately it was often darkest by the dawn. He trusted that when we had passed away from the shadow of the strike cloud, it would be seen not only to have a sil- ver lining, but to be silver through and through for that part of the community which spent its days in the most hazardous and necessary of our industries. (Applause.) Dealing with the demands of the miners, Mr. Oliver said they desired to see two amend- ments introduced in the Minimum Wage Bill. The first contained a specific clause providing that every worker, skilled or unskilled, under- ground, should have a minimum wage of ss. a day. He thought it would be found possible fOr the Government to accept such an amend- ment. ("Hear, hear.") Five shillings a day was not so much when one considered the dan- gerous occupation, and, though some people might call it revolutionary, it seemed to him that it was A SORT ()V REVOLUTION THAT WAS BOUND TO COME. (Applause.) The miners also desired to have their schedules of wages included in the Bill just as they had framed it. Personally, he thought it would be better, if it were possible, that the schedule rate for the different dis-

tricts should be settled by a conference, with an independent chairman, for the reason that such a settlement would have an added moral authority which no legislation could give it. If the miners' demands were just—and he ,be- lieved it would be found that the scheduled rates were real, genuine minimum rates—the' result of any arbitration or conference would be that they would be granted. The Govern- ment might introduce a clause guiding the chairmen in the broad principles he ought to follow in arriving at a minimum wage, and in that event the miners would probably be only 'too Willing to support the Bill in its last stages. Such a compromise would be made very much easier by the attitude which had been adopted by the Conservative party. That attitude had

• come to most of them as 'a shock. What unin- telligible reason was working in the dim and dusty minds of the Conservative party he could not for the life of him conceive; he could only think it was an example of the old tag : "Those whom the gods would destroy they first make mad." (Laughter.) It was not the first time the Conservative party had begun by saying they would help the Government to settle a national matter in a national way, and had then left them in the lurch and done everything they could to hinder them. (Ap- plause.) What alternative had the Conserva- tives to offer? It was no good for Mr. Bonar Law to laugh and say that he was not a physician and that until he was called in it was not necessary for him to prescribe. They knew he was not even the leader of his own , party—(laughter),—and so there was not much reason why he should be the physician for the nation; but in a crisis like this it was Ab- solutely absurd for a man who was supposed to be in a responsible position to act as Mr. Bonar Law, Mr. Balfour, or whoever was the leader of the Conservative party, had acted, without Offering any alternative whatever. One alternative had been suggested to him (Mr. Oliver) by a Conservative member of Par- liament, and it had also been suggested by the Standard and other Conservative papers. It was that, in order to end the struggle, the only thing the Government could do was to confiscate—at any rate, temporarily—the trade union funds, and so drive the miners, at the point of starvation, back to work. That was seriously suggested on the other side, and it gave them an insight into

WHAT TORYISM REALLY WAS (" Hears hear.") If they were going to con- fiscate the miners' funds in order to drive them to wOrk, there was other property they ought to confiscate in order to drive other people to work. (Laughter and applause.) He did not want anybody to mistake him. He was not advocating the confiscating of any property, because the Literal party believed in the sacredness of property so long as it was divested of injustice. The Liberal party, how- ever, believed that TRADE UNION FUND. WERE AS SACRED AS THE FUNDS OF MILLIONAIRE OR CAPITALIST. • (Applause.) If there was any politi- cal reason at all for the , present unrest, - continued Mr. Oliver, he did not think one had to look to Limehouse or to Mr. Lloyd George for it, but rather to fifteen years of Tory rule, in which practically nothing was done for the advancement of the cause of the people. (Applause.) It was, however, deeper than any purely political reason. The people were at last educated, and, being educated, they knew what they wanted, they realised what their position was and what it might be. As to the outcome, it might mean that those who had much would have to give up much, and perhaps to suffer something, but if it led us to a better and more stable England it would be worth all the unrest through which we were passing. (Applause.) The Liberal party could face the future with hands abso- lutely unfettered. - Unfortunately the Tory party could not. We had a new sort of Con- servative party—a DILUTED DEMOCRATIC-SCENTED CONSERVATISM. (Laughter.) It had a perfect passion for pro- gress, but it was always very much restrained by a lively feeling of its responsibility to vested interests. Its democratic enthusiasm was always tied down to the land, and its democratic ardour was considerably damped by liquor. (Laughter.) Dealing with Home Rule, Mr. Oliver said there never had been any argument against the principle which was worth knocking down. Colonel Sykes had said it was perfectly safe to give Home Rule to Canada and South Africa, because _ they were a long way off. But, he added, Ireland was right in the heart of the Empire, and therefore it would not be safe to give her Home Rule. The very fact that Ireland was so near to us, said Mr. Oliver, seemed to him the one argument which proved that it was perfectly safe to give her Home Rule. (Ap- plause.) Ireland absolutely depended upon England for everything; she was bound to us heart and soul in trade and commerce, and .her agriculture would vanish if it were not for our markets. It was absolutely essential that Ireland should remain closely embraced in the United Kingdom if she was to remain prosperous. (Applause.) Alluding to the in- troduction of the Naval Estimates, Mr. Oliver • said the discussion was a very important one, because we had shifted our ground, and now we built so as to have a 6o per cent. superi- ority over Germany. That was to say if Ger- many built five ships, we should build eight. But there was this significant announcement by Mr. Churchill—that if Germany did not build five, we. would not build eight. That was a statement which, if taken in the right spirit, might lead to a very much better state of affairs in Europe than prevailed at the present time. ("Hear, hear.") Before we got any large retrenchment in our armaments, it would be impossible for us to go on to any very extended scheme of social reform. (Ap- plause.) Mr. J. Jarman, alluding to the question of Welsh Disestablishment, said he was jn agree- ment with the Bishop of Liverpool on many matters, and he strongly approved of the bold stand which his Lordship took on the Licens- ing Bill. (" Hear, hear.") He was sorry they were on opposite sides on the Welsh Church question. If the Government dropped the question of Disendowment, did they thing the Church would worry over Disestablishment ? So far as the talk of robbery and confiscation was concerned, it should be borne in mind that the funds were not going to the endowment of Nonconformity. If the Church would be satis- fied with Disestablishment without Disendow- ment, he would say : "By all means let them keep their endowments!' The Nonconform- ists had managed without the endowments up to now, and they would still be able to manage and possibly things would go on better than they had done. (Applause.) Councillor H. Roberts, in moving a vote of thanks to the speakers, referred at some length to the antagonism of the Tory party to the rights and privileges of the people, and gave as an instance of that spirit their attitude in the present crisis. According to the news- paper reports, when Mr. Stephen Walsh, M.P., spoke in the House of Commons of miners being maimed and mutilated in hundreds of thousands, there was Opposition laughter. If the Tory members were proud of their associa- tion with that kind of indifference and apathy and contempt for the lives and bodies of work- ing men, to whom we owed so much, he did not think he was misjudging the temper of the working people ,when he said that if an election came very shortly—as it might pos- sibly do—the Tory party had sown the wind, and they would reap the whirlwind of retri- bution. (Applause.) Referring to the Con- servative party's intention to move .the rejec- tion of the Minimum Wage Bill, Councillor Roberts said he was -satisfied that there were thousands of good, honest Conservatives, who • were just as much shocked at that brutal con- duct on the part of the Leader'of the Opposi- those who were associated with th,e Opposi- tion, and of those who were following him, as were the Liberals themselves. If the electors could have canvassed on that one question, those who were associatetd with the Opposi- tion amendment would be sent to the oblivion from which they ought never to have emerged. He had thought that in Mr. Balfour they had a , man who would not have sought at a time like this, for any possible party advntage, to place _party interests ,before those of the nation as a whole. (Applause.) Mr. J. Longland seconded, and the vote Was heartily passed.

LANCASHIRE'S NEW CHIEF CONSTABLE. Mr. Harry Phillip Parnell Lane was on Thurrday afternoon appointed Chief Constable of Lancashire in succession to Captain Ibbetson, at a salary of .£l.OOO a year. Mr. Lane, who has baen Deputy-Chief Constable nearly three years, was previously Deputy-Chief Constable of Liverpool.

MARRIED WOMEN TEACHERS. Mr. Snowden, M.P., has presented a Bill to prevent the dismissal of married women teachers in schools under the control of a local education authority on the ground that they have married since their appointment, and to open the benefits of universities and colleges to women.

div.head: SENTENCES.
div.p: SENTENCES.

At the Warrington Police Police Court on Thursday, two youths, Albert Antrobus and Percy Antrobus, 70, 01 lham-street, were charged on remand with breaking In and stealin2 from the house of Mr. Arthur Rogers, postman, 99, Oldham-street, on Saturday, March 9th, a quantity of cakes and sweets.—Tne Chief Constable stated that the hou-e was left secure about 7.20 on Saturday week last, but at nine o'clock it was found that R window at the back had been broken open and the glass carefully taken out and laid on one side.—The prisoners pleaded guilty, and Albert was committed for trial at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions with a view to him being sent for a term of Borstal treatment. The younger prisoner was sent to the reformatory school until he attained the age of 19. GIRL'S INGENIOUS THEFT.

TORE COUNTERFOIL OUT OF PASS-BOOR". At the Warrington Police Court on Thursday, Winifred Brown (15), 61, Fox-street, was charged with stealing on February 22nd, £9 and a cheque for £1 12s Bd, the property of Elizabeth Hall.—The Chief Constable stated that the girl had been employed for some time by the prosecutrix, a dressmaker, who carried on business at Bold-street, and resided at Park Cottages Orford. On February 22nd, the girl was sent with nearly £lO to the bank to deposit for Miss Hall. She was given the pass book, which the bank officials were to sign on receiving the money. She went out and on her rsturn handed to Miss Hall the book, which was put on one side. On a later date when the girl was sent again Miss Hall turned up the last receipt and noticed that the signature was somewhat peculiar. When the girl returned from the bank the prosecutrix noticed that the counterfoil in the book was missing. She was taxed with the offence by the prosecutrix and she told a most diabolical story implicating another girl in the theft. She however pleaded guilty that morning. She had bought numerous articles with the money and had told an enormous amount of lies. She had purchased about £7 10s. worth of goods and stated that she had had £2 stolen from :hr. Mrs. Brown, the mother of the girl, stated that her daughter had told her that Miss Hall had given her the goods because she was leaving. The Chairman : Did you take the trouble to inquire if that was true ?—No sir.

The Chairman said it was awful to think th,it a girl of such an age should be so keen to commit a forgery and theft, accompanied by such a tissue of absolute lies. The magistrates failed to see bow the mother could be ignorant of tne fact that the girl was stealing. A fine of £5 and coats was imposed or in default two months imprisonment.

William Hall and Sous, Jockey-street, Warrington, were fined 20s. end costs for failing to have a young person medically examined and certified for employ- ment in their mineral water factory. A SPECIAL CONSTABLE'S CAPTURE.—Thomas Walton, labourer, 13, Monk-street, was charged with being on the enclosed premises of the London and North- Western Railway Company, with intent and aho charged with stealing a quantity of provisions belonging to the same Company. The Chief Constable stated that about 9.25 the previous night one of the special constables appointed to guard the railway company's property was on duty in Froghall sidings when be observed a man trying to get into a waggon. He asked him what he was doing there, and the man dropped a sack. He took him to one of the signal c,bins and subsequently the house of prisoner was searched and the whole of the provisions which included a cheese, and a case of cocoa and other eatables were found. The case was adjourned for seven days.
FRIDAY.--Before the Mayor (in the chair),!and other m.gistraees.

CRUELTY TO A HonsE.—Herhert Byron, nurseryman, Bold, St. Helens was fined lOs and costs for having causod a horse to be worked whilst in an bnfit state.—lt was stated by Inspector Lee that the animal was lame in the back leg, suffering from "ring bone." The mare was otherwise in a fair condition.

----- WIFE DESERTIoN.—LiIy Phillips, Cartwright-street, was granted a separation order with 12s per week from her husband Thomas, a wireworker, for desertion.— Defendant's only excuse was that ha could not live with her.

div.head: Borough Police Court.
div.p: Borough Police Court.
Tl:E')DAY.—Before Councillors Roberts (in the cbsir), Jackson Holmes end Mr. T. Locker.

ALLEGED THEFT OF CLOTHES.--James Ray, of no fixed abode, was charged with stealing on the previous day a suit of clothes value 12s 6sl from 100, Butter- market-street, the property of Benedict Tyrer.—The Chief Constable said P.C. Taylor saw the prisoner loitering outside Mr Tyrer's shop and acting in a suspicious manner. The officer concealed himself, and after a time 93W the defendant take a suit of clothes and bide them under his coat. The officer arrested him and took him back to Mr. Tyrer's, and it was found that the clothes had been stolen.—The case was adjourned for seven dass.

THURSDAY.—Before 3 Rymer Young (in the chair), Messrs SV It Robert, A J Jolley and Dr Naden. BREACHES OF THE FACTORIES ACT.—Thomas Astill, Green-street, Warrington, was fined 5s and costs for having on the 16th February, employed a young person in his bakery before the legal period. E E Slater, 19, Sankey-street, Warrington, was summoned for having failed to notify the inspector of the district that he had commenced to occupy a tailor's shop, and was also summoned for having employed two women after the legal period' on the 16th February.—Mr Browne, who appeared for the defendant stated that his client badcome from Cheltenham a few months ago, where it was the 'rendre for the inspector to visit the premises and the owner was not bound to advise the inspector. In the second case the women had asked to be allowed to work later and clear off a big order so that they could go home earlier on the Saturday. Defendant was ordered to pay 10.1. and costs in the first case and the costs in the second.—The Warrington Equitable Industrial Co-operative Society, Ltd., were summoned for having employed a young person in their sausage factory after the legal period on February 9th and 18th. Mr. McCaghey, LULL of Factories stated that on the 9th February a yotng person was employed from 7.45 a.m. until 12.45 a.m. the next morning—a period of seventeen hours. The hours should have been from seven to seven. In the second case the youth was working from 8 o'clock until 10.35. Mr. Jarman, secretary of the Co operative Society, said it wit, not known by the management that those hours were being kept. A fine of .£1 and costs in each case was imposed.

div.p: Warrington County Petty Sessions.
WEDNESDAY—Before Messrs Chas.Wkite.(in the chair

Henry Roberts, Roger C Parr and J Backhous-. POACHISG.—Peter Rowson, Bowes-street, was sum- moned for trespassing on land in pursuit of game.— Mr E A White, who prosecuted, said the offence was committed early in the morning of Sunday, March 3rd. The attention of a keeper named Stanley Leigh, and a youth named Harry Hutchinson, was attracted by the discharge of a gun. They saw defendant and another man on land in the occupation of John Warburton, in Moss Wood, Daßarn. Rowson was seen to pick up a kare and then he and his companion walked quickly away. The keeper followed and caught Rowson up in Winwick- road. In his breast pocket was a gun, which had been taken to pieces. The oth3r man got away.—Rowson's defence was that he left home considerably after the time when the prosecution alleged be was on the land —A fine of 405., including costs, was imposed. HAD No COAL AND STOLE TIMMS-L.—Alexander Peters, County Council roadman, Mill Cottages, Houghton Green, pleaded guilty to stealing three pieces of timber, value Is, the property of Leonard Bennett, auctioneer, Padgate-lane, Poul- ton—Accused said he had been in the habit of storing his tools in the shed from which the timber was missed and he advanced the plea that he took the wood because there was no coal in his house. He would not have taken it had he thought it was of any real value. —The Clerk (Mr H Greenall), to Mr Bennett) : I sup- pose you would have given it to him if be had ask you? Mr Bennett : I should, sir.—The Clerk (to defendant): Why didn't you ask? Defendant : Probably if I had asked him he might have given me more than I took.— Defendant was bound over in his own recognisances. THEFT Op FOWL.—Samuel Warburton, whom the police stated to be a notorious fowl thief, WAS sera to gaol for three months with hard labour for stealing six hens, value IBu., the property of Lucy Bennett, Bruche Farm, Poulton.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A.

Sunday was kept as " The National F. deration Sunday." The united societies comprise COO,OOO mem- bers in Great Britain. There are 40 Districts and County Federations, and over 2,0C0 Societies., The P.S.A. movement has extended to America, Canada, France and Belgium. This day was unitedly joined in by this great brotherhood in singing at a given time (3.30) a hymn" Fling out the banner, let it float." The meeting of the Wycliffe Society was presided over by Mr B Farrar. The ,Rev 11 Ogden, minister of the Golborne-street Baptist Church, gave an address upon " The past difficulties of the movement, the present prosperity, and the possibilities of P.S.A. men frit special work for God and men." lie said he admired that beautiful meeting and the hearty singing and devotion, and he looked further to the work being carried on during the week by good living and work- ing under the inspiration of the Sunday work. He made reference to the present coal strike and said he had sympathy for the men,who had to work under great diflmlties for a poor wage. He hoped with all in that meeting that very soon a settlement would be brought about, as the suffering of the poor must be great and would be aggravated later if peace was not restored. Mr Joseph Owen read the lesson and Mr W Beswick led a special prayer for a speedy termination of the strike. Mr Hamilton sang" s,Vhere'er you walk."

div.head: Wycliffe Cockhedge Mission.
div.p: Wycliffe Cockhedge Mission.

A grand re-union gathering was held at the above mission on Thursday evening, when about 140 friends sat down to a substantial tea provided by the ladies of the mission. The after meeting was of a social charcter, and was presided over by Mr W H Wallington the superintendent, who in a very interest- ing address on the Mission work, offered a very hearty welcome to all old friends of the Mission to come and join in the efforts that are being pat forth towards the erection of the new school to be built off Padgate-lane. Mr J Phoenix read letters of apology from various friends, who were unable to be present. An excellent programme of songs and sketches were rendered by Miss E Hewitt, Mr W Booth, Mrs Barlow and Mr S Aukland. Miss Hewitt gave a fine rendering of the song "The valley of laughter," and responding to an encore gave" My me ther bids me bind my hair," and later sang "Bid me discourse." Mr Booth, who was in excellent voice sang "Thera," " Tom Bowling," and " I seek for thee in every flower." Mr S Aukland was very happy with musical selections on his concertina, and with some very witty songs and jokes. Mrs Barlow had the audience in roars of laughter with recitations in the Lancashire dialect. Mr A Trove' was a very able accompanist. The meeting closed with a very hearty vote of thanks to the artistes by Mr G F Rushton, supported by Miss E Smith, Mr F Morrell and Mr J

div.head: Preciousness of Life.
div.p: The Preciousness of Life.

Preaching at Bold-street Wesleyan Church on Sunday morning, the Rev If Middlewood took for his text, the words " I will make a man more precious than fine gold, even a Iran than the golden wedge of Ophir." He said it was the teaching of Jesus concerning the preciousness of life and the worth of the individual that gave slay ery its death-blow, end there was nothing mote remarkable in the history of the last 100 years than the way in which slavery had been almost univer- sally abolished. There were-scenes and places where manhood was still held very cheap, but when the true meaning of the text really Sound its way to the heart of the race it would revolutionise society. It would work wonders !n relation to certain social and industrial problems of our time ; it would mean that the poor would cot be herded together in slum-dwell- ings where virtue and morality are made almost impossible ; it would mean that a terrible sweating system would he swept cut of existence, and men would no longer wear their lives away for scarcely a living wage, nor tired worn-out women sing "the song of the shirt." The homes of the twin-devils—drink and gambling—would be abolished when men bad come to know that their lives bad a value beyond all words. In the true golden age when, we have learnt this simple truth by the great Blaster taught, the cry of the children of the gutter will be heard and hushed, for men will dwell in peace together, and love, charity and brotherhood reign supreme.

div.head: Choir Festival at the Primitive Methodist Church.
div.p: Choir Festival at the Primitive Methodist Church.

Last Sunday was the choir anniversary at Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church, and proved to bean event of more than usual interest. The preacher for the day wes Rev W Cooper, who based his morning discourse upon the music rendered in Solomon's time at the dedication of the Temple. At the afternoon and even- ing services, Mr Cooper dispensed with the usual sermon and gave brief addresses upon the various selections of music. Under the capable leadership of Mr A Spruce, th 3 choir is in splendid condition, and provided a choice rendering of a carefully prepared programme. In the afternoon, Maunder's Cantata— " Penitence,Pardon and Peace," was sung with marked taste and skill, the solos being given by Miss E Hewitt Mr L Richardson and Mr N Cook, jun. Having listened to a brief exposition of the work, the congregation were better able to appreciate the Cantata, and do fuller justice to its brilliant handling by the choir. This was pre:oeded by solos from Messrs Richardson and Cook. Mr Richardson sang Dr Peace's tune to " 0 love that will not let me go," which proved to be very interesting in view of the fact that the composer had passed away only the previous Thursday morning. Before Mr. Cook's delightful rendition of Arm, arm, ye brave" from " Judas Mae,cabeus." Mr Cooper recounted the historic setting of the oratoria, which enabled the audience to catch some of the prophet': fire, so well expressed by Handel. The evening service will long be remembered. A piece from Mendelssohn's " Elijah " was interpreted by the speaker, followed by a most chaste presentation of the same piece by the choir. Two of Bernard's hymns were sung by the choir and congregation after listening to a brief biography of the poet's attainments and triumphs. Other soloists of the day were Miss Brown, Mr 0 Gough and the Messrs. Hamilton Bros. Mr F H Banner, the newly appointed organist, officiated with great credit. Mr J 11 Starkey occupied the chair in the afternoon.

div.head: St. John's Presbyterian Church.
div.p: St. John's Presbyterian Church.

Preaching from 1 Rings xii. 28, tLe Rev. W. Reid said the position taken up by the judge was that of the Monotheist and believer in the divine institution of a centralised worship. In his hatred of idolatry we could place ourselves alongside of him, but in our freedom from the ccnception of the Idealised God, asked whether Jeroboam ought not to be commended as one who went far in the direction of religious advancerr ent to break down parochial superstition? Not however, until John the Seers vision had been realized and the new earth was God-inhabited humanity,towards which all temples are,or ought to be aiming, would "no temple therein" be an accomplished fact. Spots, seasons, assemblies, etc., were still necessary to teach the holy separateness of God, and bow much more so in the day when the presence of the Canaanite in the laud brought sanctuaries and observances to be the rookeries and occasions of grossest sensuality. Jeroboam for selfish ends ignored all this, indeed lured his pelple on to it, and for the same selfish ends would use as a lever the sacred things of the higher life, and even God him- self. In failing to appreciate the values of these, and of the call addressed to Israel as a people he bartered , away a golden opportunity, and became known to posterity as the son of Nebat who made Israel to sin, Colborne-street Baptist Church. In aid of the New Building Fund of the Golborne- street Baptist Church a musical drama entitled "The Shepherds of Bethlehem" was given in the Wycliffe Memorial Hall on Thursday evening. There was a ' good attendance of about 120 persons over which the the Rev /I Ogden, pastor, !presided. The members of for the tßhaenkprQoudauyctliVo°n and Mission were responsible if the effect produced was at times contrary to their expectations, their efforts were deserving of the applause they got. The artistes who took part in the drama were :—Messrs George Dale (author of the play), Alfred Walker, Johnson Barrett, George Head, Joseph Brimelow, John Hassell, It Brimelow, Worrell, Grey, Callom, Millington and Thompson and the Misses Eva Tanner, olive Dale Charlotte Jones and Emily Dunn. Others who assisted were Messrs Albert Dale, Joseph Taylor and II Foden. Mr Tanner accompanied the vocal parts which were given in a creditable manner. A vote of thanks to the artistes proposed by the chairman was heartily given and Mr Dale suitably responded.

div.head: Cairo-street Chapel. The New Pastor's Striking Sermons. Religion and the " Social Gospel."
div.p: Cairo-street Chapel. The New Pastor's Striking Sermons. Religion and the " Social Gospel."

The Rev.Dr.Stanley A Mellor commenced his ministry at the Cairo-street Chapel on Sunday when he preached two striking sermons. Speaking in the morning on "The meaning of religion for the individual " the rev. gentleman said religion was all or nothing, MOM than a mere form, more than a parade and pretence and an accidental addition:to life. If religion was anything it was "stuff of the very stuff, life of life, and self of self," a fineness of realization which pervaded every detail of existence,not safely lobe despised or neglected or put on one side by any man desiring wholeness of life, longing for completemss and happ'ness. There was nothing paltry or mean or low in religion, nothing that should cramp or hinder the finest development of life. It was not the cover for contemptible opinions nor tin cloak of contemptible deeds ; it depended no whit upon belief or intellectual statement, but might shine and glow res.plendent when there was no knowledge and no power of utterance. In nothing did it consist more than in this ; a sense of the vast and overwhelming mystery of life, a realisation of eternal values present in the midst of temporal things, a faith in the power of thrse eternal values to make life It was no sad, unhappy, doleful exercise, but a joyous spirit that faced life eagerly end welcomed experience with shining eyes, out of conflict drawing victory, and tiading, even in the darkness, the splendour lof God. Religion was no thing for cowards or hypo- crites or mean-spirited men and women, but always and only for the brave and strong and high-spirited; for those who, even when they did not know and could not understand, were yet ready to trust their deepest instincts and to undertake the adventure of. making from their existence, no natter how humble the circum- stances and conditions, a harmony and a beauty, inward and secrini, and capable of withstanding every shock of time. Religion eas for the free soul, the finest free- dom, the noblest liberty of eternal things ; the flower of a life that rejected nothing, t.t extracted from all experience sweetness and light and joy ineffable. In the evening Dr. MELLOR took for his subject "The meaning of religion for the world," and referring to the gigantic difficuli-s.end dangers which beset our social life at the present moment he asked, would the way be so hard if every single roan concerned in those difficulties felt, burning and blazing in his own inmost heart, the intense sense of God and of a personal rela- tion with divine and eternal things? Men nowadays
OFTEN BLAMED TUE -CHURCHES and uttered criticisms against erganised religions. Only the other day, a responsible leader of many went out of his way to denounce scathingly the

div.head: WARRINGTON ‘t nur ch.
div.p: WARRINGTON ‘t nur ch.
RELIC/011S e-SOC/AL

Church and all her works. The Church might be to blame in many ways ; organised religion might be but a poor and miserable thing ; yet it in any, even in the smallest degree the Church did or could succeed in awakening the sense of personal religion in the hearts and lives of individutl men and women, she accomplished, it seemed to him, a mighty work—a work so great that, in comparison with it, all other accomplishments of human agency sank itto insignificance. The power of personal religion in the world could not be over estimated ;the value to society of one mm i utterly domiaaVd and possessed by the burning sense of God was infinite. Inward, personal religion did not take a man away from the world, it rather set him closer to it. The heart that was fired with love divine, and filled with life, remained a human heart, from which nothing human could be alien or estranged Cr distant. Much had been heard in recent years of

div.head: SOCIAL GOSPEL._
div.p: THE SOCIAL GOSPEL._

Over and over again, under the plea of making religion practical, the ministry and service of religion had been used for the partisan interference in the affairs of the world. It was true enough that, of all the great inspiring motives of mankind in the present age, none was so powerful as the social ideal, none bred such loyalty and devotion as the vision of a regenerated order of social life, and religi )11 could not be blind to that ; she must at every moment take account of the social hopes and as irations of men. But the real business of religion was not and never had been to preach a merely social gospel, to undertake definite measures of social reform, to begin this or that crusade for the economic remaking of society, to support this or that particular movement in

THE WARFARE OF POLITICS. Religious men might and must do all those things and the more the atmosphere of religion spread over them the more a orth doing would they become. The real labour of religion, however, lay elsewhere,and,from the point of view of true religion it should be said that few things had shown themselves so cheap, mean and paltry as that so-called "social gospel " by which so many bad sought mistakenly to make religion fit the times. Religion—real religion—WAS a matter of the individual soul and of the relation between the soul and God. It was a matter of attitude towards life as a whole, a thing of devotion, reverence and love. It was a seeking of satisfaction and a` desire for rest, not a rush into ceaseless activity and a never-ending weariness of toil. The great gilts of religion were made to the single individual soul. The vision and joy and glory of eternal life and love, which were the peculiar treasure of religion, were not immediately for the world or for society in the mass, but for this or that or the other longing and desiring soul that would accept the gift. Whatever her ultimate relation to social life and to the world might be, religion could not and dare not abate one whit that DEI AND INTENSE INDIVIDUALISM which was her peculiar property, that definitely personal devction, reverence, love and vision which belonged exclusively to her. For religion, the most valuable thing in the world was and must remain the individual soul with its longing for eternal things and its divine spark of eternal life. That she must seek always to cherish and cultivate and for that she must labour first and last. Religion was

NOT 71. MEANS TO TEMPORAL ENDS, even when those ends were set under the form of a perfect social ideal and perfect social order. Her object was not some future social salvation, but the saving of the individual soul here and now. Her redemptive consolatory mission was definitely to the individual soul. Christ came to save the sinful and not to remake society. Truly religion must bind her sanctity to Jill that was best in the world and in social life and in the hopes and desires that grew out of social 11f3. She must understand and boldly declare that enthusiasm for humanity was a great thing, and a thing very dole to Heaven, that loyalty to society's aims and demands, when they were set at the highest level, was a thing beautiful in itself and always to be cherished, that longing and labour for a perfect social order were, in their way and measure, longing and labour for the absolutely good and true. Religion must hearten mm—tad they needed hearten- ing—for their moral and social tasks, and so hallow and sanctify the necessary toil of humanity for humanity that it became a true spiritual adventure. She must turn men's earthly enthusiasm into heavenly devotion, change their human loyalty into Cod's own faith, and make tteir labour of duty into the labour of love. In so far forth, indeed, she must preach definitely a social gospel, and send her servants forth into the world armed in the power of social righteousness ; she could not he blind to the untruth, the injustice, the ugliness of the world, nor deaf to the appeals of ignorance, wretchedness and misery. Against all this she must speak with no uncertain voice, but the words she used must be drawn always from that pure realm of eternal things which knew nothing of merely partisan and

sectarian differences. Yet that was not the end of her work, nor indeed the chief part of her labour. That was still to be found in her dealings with the individual soul. Here she must save, inspire and uplift.

div.head: DR. MELLOR WELCOMED.
div.p: DR. MELLOR WELCOMED.

Monday was a day of welcome for the new pastor of the Unitarian Cairo-street Chapel, the Rev Stanley A Mellor, It A., Ph. D. The meeting was held in the schoolroom and was very well attended by members of the congregatiou. Mr F W Monks presided and was supported on the platform by Dr Mellor, Messrs J Rymer Young, J W Davies (church secretary), D Plinston (superintendent of the Sunday school), W H Drummond, London (a late pastor of Cairo-street), Rev E Stanley Russell (Liverpool), Rev W Whittaker (Manchester) and Rev W Reid (Warrington). Among others present were :—Messrs W Ii Woodcock,H Noble and J 8 Hill.

The SECRETARY read letters of apology from the following :—Revs ft Nicol Cross (Southpsrt), J Lloyd Thomas (Nottingham), %V A Beckett (Bewsey-road, Warrington), J Yonge (Wycliffe, Warrington), C Peach, and one from Mr F E Brookbank (secretary of the Rotherham Church). The CHAIRMAN said that the absence of Mr Long through indiffereet health would be regretted by them all. He was sure that both he and Mrs Long bad their warmest sympathy. He (Mr Monks) was very glad to be occupying the chair under such pleasant circum- stances. He was pleased also to see such a good gathering, and especially so many young people. It argued well for the churche's future, and he felt doubly sure that it would inspire their new pastor Dr Mellor. (Applause.) Mr J Rymer Young said that be had been asked to welcome Dr Mellor on behalf of the congrega- tion. To he the mouthpiece of so fine an audience as the one gathered there,was to him a very pleasent duty. It was a year since the passing of their late respected and esteemed minister, the Rev C Harvey Cook, and during that year they had been like a flock of sheep without a shepherd. He was inclined to think it was a mistake to allow such an interval to elapse, as church matters were liable to become a little slack. He could assure them that the selecting of a minister was in no way an easy task. They had, however, tested and tried Dr Mellor, and like the water analyst they were able to report—free from all traces of impurity' (Laughter.) He (Nlr Yonge) was impressed by Dr. Stellor's services on Sunday last. He hoped that they would grant his requests, and give him a good moral backing. (Applause.) He believed Dr. Mellor proposed at an early date to take another important step, and it would be their duty, when the lady came into their midst, to give her also a sincere welcome. (Applause.) It was, however, their first duty, and he was also sure it was their desire to accord Dr. Mellor a hearty and unqualified welcome. (Applause.) The Rev NV REED welcomed Dr Mellor on behalf of himself and congregation. This he dfli with a feeling of gratitude, for it was the good people of Cairo-street who had helped his people and given them as it were, a place to rest the sole of their foot,when no one else had done. There in the room where they were assembled his people had met and worshipped. There also they had met and talked matters over until they could decide to launch out. And they all knew the gratify- ing result of the kindness of the Cairo-street people, for they were now well-established. (Applau.e.) He took that opportunity of thanking them. Mr Reid reminded Dr Mellor that with the exception of the Rev John Yonge, he had been in the town longer than any other Free Church minister, although he only came three years ago. There was a great sphere of work for them all in the town, and it was gratifying to know that the Free Churches were drawn together more closely than in bygone days. (Applause). Mr. PLINSTON, as superintendent of the Sunday school, heartily welcomed the new pastor. A wise pastor would give his chief attention to the young, because the children of the present day were the people upon whom they would have to depsnd in the future. Continuing Mr. Plinston said that Dr. Mellor bad already created a good impression in the school. He had inspired them and they were looking forward to good work being done through his able and generous assistance. (Applause). The Rev. E. STANLEY RUSSELL welcomed Dr. Mellor to the district on behalf of the Churches in the Liver- pool district. He believed he would be a very great asset and acquisition to the Liverpool District Missionary Association. (Rear, hear.) Dr. Mellor was a man who would give a distinct religious tone to any district in which he might be, and would be a great fore?. (Applause). The Rev. W. WsirmaKert, on behalf oy the Churches in the Manchester district, said Dr. Mellor was not only a young man, but one who had new things to say, and in saying them he might be misundersteol. He pleaded for tolerance, believing that Dr. Mellor's only desire would be for the furtherance of their cause, and that of religion generally. (Applause). The Rev. W. H. DRUMMOND, a former min'ster of the church, said it was almost nineteen years since they held a similar meeting to welcome him into their midst. Dr. Mellor was to be congratulated upon coming to a place like Warrington so early in his ministry. Cairo- street Chapel was apiece with fine traditions, and Dr. Mellor came as a well-equipped successor to those who had gone before. (Applause). A little while before coming, he (Mr Drummond) had been talking to a friend about %Varrington. He told this friend that he was going to Dr. Mellor's welcome, and so, Mr. Drummond, his father replied " Dr. Mellor ought to do good work in Warrington. (Applause.) The speaker urged Dr. Mellor to be a great pastor, to get into the homes of the people and leaf n of their difficulties sod trials. It was only by so doing that a minister of God was able to pray, well knowing from experience what to pray for. To Dr. Mellor he extended a most cordial welcome. (Applause). Mr COCKER, of Rotherham, said Dr Mellor was held in high esteem in the town he had just left and was ' quite deserving of that esteem. He would be missed, I not only by his old congregation, but by many belong- ing to other churches. Since Dr. Mellor had gone he I (Mr Cocker) had been frequently stopped by friends who expressed regret at his departure (Applause). Dr. Mes Lott, in reply, thanked all present for tha heartiness and genuineness of their welcome. He felt drawn towards the chapel from the first moment he was asked to preach in it. The chapel and school buildings suggested opportunities. He admired the great tradi- tions of the chapel and liked the fine free Presbyterian ancestry which belonged to it. Ile felt attracted to Warrington because of its connection with Manchester College, Oxford, which movement almost began in the town, and from which he learned to value and to under- stand the traditions of freedom in which they were brought up. (Applause ) The congregation at War- rington had always been regarded as one of the finest and best, and he believed there was a great work to be done in the town. If they were loyal to him and he , was loyal to them they would do something which was worth doing and of which they would all be proud. (Applause). During the proceedings, the choir interspersed a few fine selections, and they were ably conducted by the I organist and choirmaster Mr. J. M. Muir.

div.head: Hill Chile Baptist Church.
div.p: Hill Chile Baptist Church.

On Thursday last a pleasant social gathering was held at the above church, considerably over 100 members of the church and congregation being present. Solos were rendered by Miss A Grounds and Miss Sherwood. Much amusement was created by two dialogues given by the "Hill Cliffe Dialogue Party." Miss A Grounds and Miss Healey and 51esars J Roughsedge, G Ault, G MOH, and P Moss. The proceeds were for the ladies sewing ohm (which will be held on Tuesday afternoons). Refreshments were served during the evening. The successful and enjoyable gathering was brought to a close at ten o'clock by singing the doxology.

div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.
WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S ASSOCIATION
(N.A. CENTRE).

Close season has arrived, and the set boards are not up to the usual standard, leaving the set money to be competed for when we o,3en again. The heaviest three roach records are : lib loz ; 15n 14drs ; 150 z 4ths I respectively—not a great lct to beat, especially when we had roach well over the pound during last summer months. Although the top three roach come from the Gowy, taking the amount of angling that has been done there i this winter t has been very poor sport for weighers, especially when we look back no later than last year and find roach recorded up to ills7oz. However, competi- tion being more open, members may take advantage of it and try all the more to lower the specimens caught during the back end. Several anglers visited the Gowy right up to the last day open for them but sport was very poor, the largest roach taken only weighing 10oz. I We do not hear of a great number of anglers anxious I to go out for Pike flounder trout or eels. They may be waiting for the weather to come warmer. Eels have been caught weeks ego in the Go fly, but I would not venture to say they are yet on the run in the canals. The open match at Norton was discussed last com- mittee night but the matter was lert over till the month of April the opinion of the committee being open as to the amount to be competed for.

N.A.A. A report of an interview between a committee of the Lune fishery Board and two representatives of the N.A.A. (Messrs. Redford sad Fletcher) with reference to licence duties, resulted in the concession by the Fishery Board of the right of fishing with shilling licences in the Calder, Broch, and other streams any- where below the Lancaster Canal. Centre secretaries please note : An application from Bradford Centre to be allowed to issue fishing tickets on the Leeds and Liverpocl Canal at :id. each, the purchasers to become entitled to membership of one of the clubs when they have taken a sufficient number of tickets, was deferred in the absence of the representative. The Shropshire Union Canal Company has decided to maintain the full close season. The Lancaster Canal Manager has consented to open at Whitsuntide as usual. A. S.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, Match, 23, 1912.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, Match, 23, 1912.
AN AI,MOST FORGOTTEN GENIUS.

It is even more unfortunate that none of Liverpool's sons thought it worth while to tell posterity anything about Thomas Steers. The little that we know has to be gleaned from the bald and unromantic records of the Council and can be put in a sentence or two. During his term as Dock Master he con- structed not only the Old Dock, but the Canning and Salthouse Basins, and he was architect of St. George's Church which stood on the site of Liverpool Castle, and was removed a few years ago to give place to the Victoria Memorial. He was the architect, too, of Liverpool's first theatre opened in 1749 and which stood in the Old Ropery. Beyond this Liverpool knows little of its pioneer. It has reared him no monument and save for a fresco recently painted on the walls of the Kardornah Cafe we know of nothing that perpetuates his name. The name of George Stephenson is upon the roll of fame, yet who would say that Stephenson did as much for commerce as Thomas Steers? Without the dock it is not conceivable that our modern system of trading could have come into being, and it seems little less than a tragedy that his name should have been left in obscurity and his history irrecoverably lost. Not that Thomas Steers lacked the appre- ciation of his fellows. The records say that a Thomas Steers was Bailiff in 1719 and 1731. and Mayor in 1739, and we may presume that this was our hero. Perhaps a patient historian may someday glean information enough to write a brief biography. And if someone will discover to us his grave we may lay a wreath when 1915 brings the second centenary of his great achievement. .

Until then our homage must be to a shadowy and modest figure whose pound7a- week salary is the most substantial thing we know of him. But docks the world over are his memorial, and we will not forget him. Honour to Thomas Steers! A.M.

HOW TO FORETELL THE WEATHER. Now that spring is close upon us we shall be thinking about our outdoor excursions and amusements, and my readers may be glad if I give them a few more hints upon the sub- ject of foretelling the weather. A weather glass is of course the best guide, but there are very many other things that give indica- tions as to rain and sunshine, and it is most interesting to watch them. I am going to mention a few. If small black clouds be seen in an other- wise clear blue sky, or if, at sunset, such clouds stand out in front of other and lighter clouds, rain may be expected ere long. But if masses of snow-white fleecy clouds rise rapidly in the sky, ever changing their shapes and disappearing, fair weather is certain. In summer,a heavy night-dew always pro- claims a fine day, but if several such dews be followed by a complete absence of dew, a rainy day may be looked for. A misty morning in autumn may portend brilliant sunshine or pitiless rain, but should dew laden spider-webs cover grass and shrubs, warm sunshine will burst forth. In winter, if a frost follows heavy rain, almost always succeeds three white frosts. The proverbs that "A black frost is a long frost " is most reliable. Animals and birds are acutely affected by the weather and a careful study of their ways will provide many signs of the approach of change. Nature seems to have endowed them with a keen weather sense, for their welfare, and even their very lives, may depend upon such fore-knowledge. In this connection, the following are deserving of attention as indicating rain : Sheep stand with their tails towards the winds. Bees fly but a little way or stay at home. 1 Gnats and flies are a nuisance and sting sharply. Flies collect indoors. Swallows fly low in the evening, for their chief foods, gnats and flies, remain near the ground when the upper air is damp. Sea-birds fly inland. Rabbits, which much dislike rain, feed in the fields in the afternoon, instead of at night as is their natural habit. Rooks remain n?ar their rookeries, instead of flying afar as they do when fair weather is in prospect. Fish swim very near to the top of the water. Other effects, due to the presence of con- ' siderable moisture in the air, which indicate rain are : A ring round the moon. Indoor walls moist. The beating down of smoke. The tightening of a rope previously slack. Smells of all kinds very noticeable. Seaweed damp. A very faint yellow sunset. A very clear distant view. "Red in the morning is the shepherd's warning." A. FINE DODGER. Carol's grandfather had served in the civil war, and Carol liked to hear of the many battles in which he had fought. One day, after listening to the vivid recital of many heroic deeds, Carol said Grandfather, you went through all those battles ? " " Yes." "And the shot and shell fell all around you?" " Yes." "And soldiers were falling and dying everywhere?" " Yes."

"Well, grandfather, what a fine dodger you must have been!" MR. CAN'T AND MR. CAN. Oh, Mr. Can't from Mr. Can Is a very different sort of man. For Mr. Can he always tries, Aid Mr. Can't he always cries ; Now Mr. Can gets many a blow, But he gets the best in the end, you know. While Mr. Can't gets nothing at all— For he's down too low to suffer a fall, Oh, Mr. Can gets up with a grin, And he says : " l'm bound in the end to win." But, Mr. Can't is a pitiful sight. For he's whipped before he's begun to fight ; And he says it puzzles him quite a lot, Why some can win and some can not. Oh, poor Mr. Can't he never knew, The secret I'm going to whisper to you; That you can win if you only try, Ard you certainly can't if you only cry, And that is the reason why Mr. Can From Mr. Can't is a different man.

div.head: PLAYING HAMLET.
div.p: PLAYING HAMLET.

The actor Salvini has often told how he was once booked to play Hamlet in London, but on arrival learnt that Irving was performing in the sgme play, and he therefore asked his manager to cancel Hamlet from his repertoire, but he would Lot do so. One evening, two days before Signor Salmi was to appear in the part, he bought a ticket for the gallery and went to see Irving. He said to himself," I will not play Humid.! " After the second scene, he said the same thing; but when the act came with Ophelia and the closet scene with the Queen, he said to himself, " I will play Hamlet! " I have my.elf said time after time, "I will not spell Shakespere as the maj rity spell it, because I am satisfied that it is not the correct way." I have concluded, however, that it is not of sufficient importmce to make it worth while to "play Hamlet" about it—nor would it be even were I of EU fficient importance to dogmatise upon the pJint.

SUNDAY OBSERVANCE. In view of the action taken by the Lord's Day Observance Society as reported in the opening para- graph of last week's Church News, I recall that, in connection with Mr. Irving's plea awhile ago for Sunday performances of Shakespeare—it was noted, as a matter of historical interest, that it is quite prob- able that some, if not the nrijority of the great master's plays were performed for the first time on Sunday afternoons. In Elizabethan times Sunday was the favourite day for the presentation of new pieces at the. theatres. The early " first-night" perform- ances commenced at 1 p.m., and generally lasted until five or six o'clock. Double prices were charged for admission—a fact which warrants the inference that these Sunday performances were well patronised. Even then, however, there was evidently a strong feeling against the practice. The corres- pondent whom I quote pointed out that when the fall of a scaffold during a public ante' tainment at the Paris uarden, Bankside, one Sunday afternoon in 1582 resulted in the loss of several lives, the Lord Mayor described the accident in his report to Lord Burkigh as "a well-merited judgment of heaven for the violation and desecration of the Sabbath." Just as the Lord's Day Observance Society now appeals for sermons on the subject of Sabbath desecration, so did the pulpit protest in Elizabethan times. Here is an extract from a deliverance by John Stockwood at St. Paul's Cross:—" Will not a fylthye plage with the blaste of a trumpette sooner call thyther a thousande than an houres tolling of a bell bring to the sermon a hundred. . . . If you resirte to the theatre, the curtayne, and other places of players in the citie, you shall on the Lord's Day have these places, with many other that I can reckon, so full as possible they can throng." We have not quite got back to that state of things yet. TREATMENT OF VAGRANTS. As to this, we do not brand with hot irons the incorrigible vagrant, as in "the spacious days of , great Elizabeth ' and especially in the old times before them. I wonder what a Workhouse master like Mr. J. F. Awbery w uld have done had he lived at a former period, and been required to torture con- firmed tramps. And yet I dare say that wonderfully tender-hearted and conscientious Poor Law official will agree with Miss Edith Sellara when she submits (as she did not very long ago in a " Cornhill " article on the ideal casual ward) that no man ought to be allowed to enter any such ward unless he can prove that he has been in regular work within three months; I this is a rule in force in all Continental casual-wards, and it works easily and well. No man ought to be allowed to cross tbe threshold of any such place if he is known to have been drunk while professing to look for work, to have refused work offered him under fair conditions. Casual-ward doors should be closed inexorably against the whole work-shirking tribe, if only for the sake of the work-seeker. A psnal colony, or a prison, is the place for a work-shirker a casual- ward ought to be kept as a refuge to which decent men, when overtaken by misfortune, may go without lcsing their self-respect. Otherwise it serves no useful purpose at all, and the money spent on it is wasted. A casual ward ought not to be a place where men are pauperised, but a place where they might be assured of help in all possible ways to struggle against pauperisation. THE IRREPRESSIBLE DARKEY. div.head: WORKS FATALITY. Youth Whirled Round a Shafting.
div.p: WORKS FATALITY. Youth Whirled Round a Shafting.

The fatality which occurred at the works of Messrs. Joseph Crosfleld and Sons, Ltd., on Friday of last week, when Stephen Barnes, aged 19 years, of 2, Friar's.lace, was whirled round a shafting, was inquired into by Mr S Brighouse, county coroner, at the Warrington Police Station on Tuesday. Mr F It Roberta appeared for Messrs Crosfleld and Mr Knowles for the relatives of Barnes, and Mr W .1 McCaghey, ILM.I , was present. John Barnes, brother of the deceased, said he went to the Infirmary shortly after the accident on Friday, and his brother said to him: "lam in luck's way. Broken leg, ribs crushed, nine stitches in my head. I don't know how it happened." Thomas Heatou, Priestley-street, stated that on Ftiday morning he was working in the same room with Barnes. fie saw him got on a bench and commence to clean the drip tin which hung beneath the bearings of a revolving shaft. He (witness) asked him to come down, and he saw a man named Taylor get on the bench to assist Barnes. The next thing he heard a shout, and saw Taylor fall off ths bench and Barnes being carried round the ahafriug. The machinery was stopped and Barnes was removed to the Infirmary. lie thought Barnes had noticed oil coming from the drip tin and had tried to clean it.

In answer to the Coroner, witness slid it was not part of Barnes' duty to clean the drip tin while the machinery was in motion. If anything was wrong it should be reported to the foreman. The Coroner : This was Z3fti on the part of the man. He had nothing to do, and thought he would rectify the matter?

Witness : Ycs, sir. In answer to Mr. McCaghey, witnms said he never saw the deceased or any other man doing similar work. Fred 'relor, a tin-box maker, said Barnes wailed to him to hold a tin whilst he empted the drip tin into it. Barnes was standing on some wooden railings facing h f the shafting,which was revolving,and witness the end f' don the bench. He heard a shout, and on looking up saw Barnes fast on the chartings and as be was whirling round his legs caught witness and knocked him down.

Robert Walker' Neston-street, said it was his duty to attend to all thebearings about the place,which he did while the machinery was stopped during the dinner hour. The deceased had no right to attend to the drip tin because it wcks not his duty. Ile might have done it to save the trouble of bringing sometme else. Witness had not noticed any drippings on the Thursday when he inspected the tin. A verdict of " Accidental death "was re:urntd. . .
Mr. McCagbey said the arrangements at Meisrs. Crosfields were as good as they could possibly be. Mr. Roberts expressed the regret of the firm at the accident.
Mr. Knowles, on behalf of the relativeq, thanked Messrs. CroEfield's for their expressions of regret.

TILE CANADIAN OFFICIAL INDEX NUMBER of whole sale prices for January stood at 1311, compared with 1294 the preceding month, and 1263 in the correspond- ing month last year. The numbers,it will be understood, are percentages in each case of the average price level prevailing during the decade, 1890-1899, the period selected by the Department as the standard of compari- son throughout its investigation into wholesale prices Some 250 articles, earefully selected to represent Canadian production and consumption, are included in the calculation. The chief increases during the past year occurred in grains and folders, dairy products, fish, fruits and vegetables and metals ; there having been decrecses in animals and meats and paints and oils. The feature of January were advances in grains and fodder, lanimals awl meats, dairy produce with slight declines in fruits and vegetables and miscellaneous groceries.

div.head: WELSH DISESTABLISHMENT.
div.p: WELSH DISESTABLISHMENT.
PROTEST MEETING AT THE PARR HALL
"SACRILEGIOUS HANDS UPON THE TREASURY OF GOD."

" A blunder and a crime " is the Bishop of Liver- pool's description of the proposed Disestablishment and Disendownient of the Church in Wales. His lord- ship presided at a meeting of protest held in the Parr Hall on Monday evening by the Churchpeople of Warrington and delivered an address in which he characterised the effect of the proposed Bill as the laying of "sacrilegious hands upon the treasury of God." The other speakers it the meeting were the Bishop of Llandaff and Mr. E. W. Johnson, a Weleh laymen. Tie hall was well filled and on the platform was a large gathering of clergy and prominent laymen, including the Rector (the Rev. Canon Willis), the Rev. Canna Penrhyn, the Rev. Canon Morley Stevenson, and Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., C.V.O. The Blsitor OF LIVERPOOL raid that magnificent meeting on such a night, in the midst of a coal strike, was evidence of the warmth of Church feeling in Warrington. Defining the character of the meeting his lordship said that party politics had there no place. The Disestablishment and Disendowment of the Church in Wahs was opposed by men belonging to every political party in the State. Many of its strongest adversaries were Liberal Churchmen. Their object was not to embarrass or to weaken the Government of the day at a most critical and difficult time but only to protest with all their might against the proposal to cripple and to despoil that part of the National Church ahich works in Wales. The question went far de3per then party politics. It affected the well-being of religion. Nor was their meeting inspired by any dislike or antagonism to Nonconformity. They gladly and ungrudgingly acknowledged the excellent work which Nonconformists were carrying on in many parts of this country. Thy freely admitted that in days when the Church in Wales was asleep they kept the flag of Christianity flying and tho light of Christianity burning in many places. They certainly most deeply regrettedthe attitude of large numbe-s of Nonconform'st both in Wales and out of it t ) the National Church, and their determination to deprive her of a largo part of her endowments ; but not one harsh word would be spoken against Nonconformity as such. They knew that many religiously-minded and right-thinking Nonconformists were exceedingly uneasy at the attack made upon the Church, and that their dissatisfaction was spreading and deepening. (Applause.) Letters which bad recently appeared in the " Manchester Guardian " had shown us what was in the minds of many of the Nonconformists !eiders. Nor in the third place were they there merely to defend the Church in Wales, but to guard the Clutch of England as a whole of which the four Welsh Dioceses were an integral part —the poorest if they liked, but the most ancient. (Applayse.)On the authority of Mr Gladstone it was as historically true to talk about the Church of Wales in England as about the Church of England in Wales. The two could not be separated. All the arguments alleged to-day in favour of the Disestablishment and the Discndowment of the Church in Wales applied with equal cogency to the Church of %gland. He would characterise the proposed Bill in a sentence—to pass it would be

A BLUNDER AND A CRIME. (Applause.) It would be an act as irrevocable as the breaking of an egg, as tte spilling of water on the ground, as death itself. It could not be undone. It would do good to no-one. It would not only he use- less but mischievous. It would weaken the Church itself just at a moment when it was seeking faithfully to fulfil its mission, when it was making rapid progress, and proving a growing blessing to the country,especially to the large towns and not least to the parishes in which there was no resident Nonconformist minister. According to Mr Asquith's last Bill, the Church was to be despoiled of 18s 6d out of every sovereign of the endowment which it possessed. In the new Bill to be introduced into the House of COMMGII9 within the next few days, we were informed that the grants from the Ecclesiastical Commissioners and from Queen Anne's Bounty were still to be continued to the Church,ao that instead of being left is 6d in the .0 it might possibly be allotted 5i in the .C. By the first Bill a Vicar in Wales in receipt of £l5O a year would have had his income reduced to something like £ll ss, or 43 3d a week. By the tew Bill he would receive £37 lOs a year, or 15s or 163 a week,while in 500 out of the 1,983 parishes in Wales, the incumbents would receive smaller pittances still. Just at a time when the Government had endowed members of Pailiament—(applause)—and were about to introduce a Bill

INSISTING ON A MINIMUM 'A'AGB for our won,ers—(applause)—and none of them grudged it—they would take ars ay what was not even s minimum wage from the clergy of the Church in Wales. (Applause.) The withdrawal of three-quarters of her inzome would mean that the Church must lose a very large proportion of her clergy; that she must contract her activities, and cut down her beneficent work at the very moment when her influence was more power- fully felt than it had been for a century and a half, and when the country needed her most. It would be

DISASTER TO WALES itself. The Welsh people were essentially religious, but there were not, wanting signs that a change was coming over their. While the Church was growing in numbers and in influence the Nonconformist bodies were losing ground. The younger generation of Welsh people were breaking loose from their old traditirms. A spirit of unrest and lawlessness was beginning to show itself in Borne districts, and slatistios seem to show that the moral standard of the people trim by no means rising and called for serious consideration. And just at the moment when the forces of religion and morality were showing signs of weakness this terrible blow was about to be inflicted on, what was after all, the largest religious body in Wales and the most powerful and progressive. (Applause.) Such a step would leave behind ita Litterness which it would take generations te wipe out and would place that unity for which they all longed at a far distant day in the future. Not least the attack on the Church in Wales, if successful, would inflict a severe blow on religion. Its moral effect would be felt not only in England but throughout Europe. Our great dependencies in the Far East would hear of it and lay it to heart. We had recently beard how pro- foundly India had been inreseed by the scrupulous attention paid by our King and Queen during their recent tour to all the outward observances of religion. Vast crowds watched them going up to worship God in stately cathedral or little garrison church, and learnt with something like awe that

THE KING OF ENGLAND was to be seen kneeling upon his knees and worshipping the King of Kings. When it became known among them that that very King's Parliament had decreed that the State in one part of the United Kingdom should cease to recognise religion, and had transferred from the temples of Christianity to mere secular purposes money left in psst years for the service of God, our hold upon them as a religious people would be seriously impaired and a new obstacle be created in the progress of the Christian faith. Be was convinced that a large umber of religiously-minded people were supporting the proposed Bill became they believe that they were doing G d's service. He could not, however, under- stand their pobiticn. He could only attribute it to inadequate knowledge, and to quote Bishop Butler, to "shortage of thought." For his own part he should regard himself as

div.head: ROBBING_ GOD
div.p: ROBBING_ GOD

if he transferred, or supported the tranference of money left for God's work to any religious body to secular purposes. It was a truism that Parliament had absolute povicr over every kind of property. Thera were times when Parliament must interfere and change the use of moneys left for religious or charitable purposes. When, for instancp the needs for which that money was left had ceased to exist or when the objects bad been neglected and forgotten and the trmit had been misused or abused,then he held that the State had a right to step in and either see that the trustees fulfilled their trust or transferred it to other objects. But in the case of the Welsh Church the Trust was being carried out. The money was being put to the very purposes for which it was intended. It was being well used. For Parliament to step in and with one fell swoop to deprive a living, I working, fruit-bearing Church of say £200,000a year was in his opinion, a crime. (Applause). For whence did I the money come? It was boldly declared to belong to the State. It was

NEITHER OIVEN TO THE STATE NOR BY THE STATE. The endowments of the Church in Wales, like those of the Church of England, were given by godly Church- men for the benefit of the Church in certain neighbour- hoods. Sometimes they were given in the form of money, sometimes of land, and sometimes of tithes, a charge or rent upon the land ; and when the State legalised the payment say of the tithe and made it com- pulsory it did not thereby become the owner of the tithe any more than when it legalised the payment. of "ground rents, it became the owner of the ground rents. These endowments bad been held in many instances for hundreds of years. He always understood that the more ancient the payment the better the title (Applause). And it must be remembered that if the Church were disendowed tithes would still have to be paid, but they would be diverted from the service of the Church. Such a crime was sure sooner or later to bring its own retribution. 1 here wrs an dd Greek story of an eagle which hovering over a temple, suddenly swooped down upon the sacrifice as it burnt on the altar and carried it off to its nest to feed its young, and with the sacrifice derply embedded in the flesh it carried a live coal which fired its nest and destroyed its eaglets. Even Greek 1 heathenism would teach us that he who robbed God •could sooner or later find his spoil a curse and not a blessing. And tc-day when in ignorance and want of thought sacrilegious hands were laid upon the treasury of God, it was for those who honoured God and loved His Church to say 'see that ye rob not the Most High lest ye be cursed with the curse." (Applause). Mr. E. W. JOHNSON !moved a resolution expressing the opinion that the Dises'ablishment and Disendos- ment of the Church in Wales and the secularization of funds given to and urgeutly needed for religious pur- poses would be aninjustice to the Church end injurious

div.p: DECORATION.
