KING STREET, MANCHESTER.

to the cause of Christianity in general. If the nation had any interest in Church prorerty it was cnly that of a trustee to see that the money was religiously applied to the purposcs for which it was originally given and which existed with greater force than ever to-day. The present generation had no right to put an. end to

div.head: PERPETUAL TRUST
div.p: A PERPETUAL TRUST

and to say that future generations were to forfeit their share in the magnificent privileges which it conferred (Applause). Mr McKenns, in his Queen's Hall speezdt, told us that Disestahlishment and Disendow. went of the kind now proposed had been carried out. in the case of the Irish Church. Why could not these eminent men tell us the whole trit'..6 ?Did Mr. McKenna tell us that only three per cent, of the total population of Ireland were adherents of the National Courch at that time ? Did be tell us that the total endowments of the Church in Ireland at that time were about £ t 6,000,000 and that £ 1,000,000 —more than the Church in Wales ever bad—ware left to her ? Did he tell us that £2,700,000 was given out, of the other £5,000,000 to the Irish Presbyterians? Did he tells us, last but not least, that the Church in Ireland was united with the great old National British Church by an Act of Parliament ? The Church in Wales claimed no life from any Act of Parliament. (Applause.) The National Church was there long before the days of Parliament. (Applause ) Did the advocates of disestablishment ever tell us that the percentage of Sunday school scholars and communicants of the Church was slightly greater in Wales than in England? Did they tell us that the Church was the only progressive religious irstitution in the Principality, or that they bad more than once refused the challenge to go to the people of Wales and ass them, by a referendum or census, uhether they were in favour of the Bill ? (Applause.) They knew what tho result would be. (Applause.) Some of the Nonconformist ministers and many of the politicians might want what they called religious equality, but on that point they did not represent the people of Wales. (Applause). Tbe Brsnor or LANDAFF then gave a very compre- hensive address. He said that if the people of Lanca- shire stood by the Church of Wales the cause would be won, for " what Lancashire thinks to-day, England thinks to-morrow." (Applause.; Ile submitted that to lower the status and weaken the position of the National Church in the ways proposed would be an injury to the State, even more than to the Church, and would tend to

LOWER THE NATIONAL SENSE OF RIGHT, to deaden the national conscience and to degrade the national character. (Apr,lau:e.) ft was hard indeed if the Church was now to be punished for failures which were largely due to the mistaken policy of English statesman of a past age—failures which were novr being rapidly turned into successes. (Applause) He had lived all his life in Wales, for the most part in thickly populated industrial centres of South Wales, and counted many Nonconformist ministers and laymen among his personal friends, lie had no heAtation in saying that he did not believe for a moment that the vast majority of Welshmen had any rooted antipathy either to the principle of an Established Church or to the actual Church which was now Established.(Applause.) He granted there were some who had such antipathy, but he believed their number was comparatively small and it was certainly diminishing. It was proved by the recent Royal Commission that the Church in Wales was for stronger numerically, in geographical prevalence and in activity and life than any other single religious body in Wales. (Applause.) They were told that the Object was to strengthen and purify the Church by separating it from its unholy alliance with the State. He believed there were some really honest and sincere Christian people who took that view and they had a perfect right to their own opinions, but personally be ventured very disrespectfully to differ from them. If it was entirely , for the good of the Church that it should be dis- established, would it not be fair and reasonable that Churctipeople should have some voice in the matter and that their opinion should have some little weight ? If it was wrong in principle that there should be any I alliance between Church dud State, was it not equally wrong in England ? %Vhy should Wales be treated differently from England ?Was that religion.; equality ? If it was a good thing for Churchmen in Wales that , they should be cut off from their brethren in England and forced into a separate organisation, would it not be qually goo 4 for the Nonconformist bodies ? (Applause). Why should they try to force upon Church- men, with the help of the secular arm and by the votes of men whose religious opinions they rejected, a separa- tion which they themselves refused with scorn ? (Applause). If the measure were passed, it would inevitably create in the minds of the great mass of Churchmen a bitter sense of wrong and injustice perpe- trated at the instigation and with the co-operation of I their brother Christians. His lordship made a strong appeal to Christians who were tempted to engage in INTERNECINE SUICIDAL WARFARE

tot to turn their weapons upon cne another, but to stand shouldtr to shoulder against the advancing hosts, on whore banners might be seen the symbols of the powers of darkness, whose onward course was marked by the spread of intemperance, impurity, irreligion, lawlessness and violence, which brought in its train darkness, misery and despair. If the disendowment proposals took effect MI out, of 983 parishes in Wales would be left without one penny of endowment, while 132 would be left with less than £lO a year. Was that right, honourable or expedient? (" No.") Having dealt with the progre-,s of Church life in his own diocese, the Bishop said they bad a vast and growing population,

_ _ SEETHING WITH UNREST, stirred with ail the eager quFstionings of the day on matters social, educational, tnoral and religious. In the midst of that great populsta?n they had a struggling Christian community, steadily winning its way to the hearts of the people who were responding in increasing numbers year by year to the call to a higher, nobler and more unselfish life. Now in the midst of its greatest activity, and in the day of its greates promise of increasing usefulness, that Christian community was to be attacked and crippled and turned away from its work of beneficence to a ttruggle for bare existence. (Applause). The resolution was carried with one dissentient.

Mr. WEST/3(200K, in moving a vote of thanks to the speakers, said Churchmen in England were not pre- pared to stand quietly by and see their brethren in Wales pillaged and plundered. Mr. W. H. STANSFIRLD seconded. Ile said be did not believe that the people of England wero TeL ma degenerate as to pass such a wicked measure if they only knew the truth about it. (Applause). lrhe Rev.Jose.mr HowArtn,retired Wesleyan minister, in supporting, said the question was not a sectional or denominational matter but a national and vital thing. As a minister of a sister Church, he concurred with everything that had been advanced by the speakers. Of all the mad schemes, the present one was about the most arrogant and (be most sinful that his mind could conceive. Why cripple the Church of England at a time when she seemed to be realizing the greatness of her own strength and making efforts to cope with missionary problems ? He could not do it, as a member of another Church ; he would rather lose everything he possessed. The Church would have his prayers and his interest in every possible way, both of mind and of purse, because he owed very much as a minister of the Gospel to her saintly men. (Applause.) The vote was heartily carried.

div.p: OPERATION ON LADY CREWE.

The Marchioness of Crewe underwent an operation for appendicitis at her London residencN Crewe House, on Monday. The operation was successful, and the Marchioness passed a fairly good night, and was yester- day progressing favourably. As late as Friday last Lady Crewe attended their Majesties' Court at Buck- ingham Palace and made a number of presentations.

div.head: GREAT INSURANCE
div.p: THE GREAT INSURANCE
ACT.
A GENERAL SURVEY.
BY RIGHT HON. T. J. MACNAMARA, M.P. SECRETARY TO THE ADMIRALTY.

We have undertaken a colossal task; and at every stage of that task our purpose has been patriotism before popularity. We took stock of the condition of the people. We saw the ravages of sickness that could be cured and might be prevented. We saw the misery in- flicted by unemployment, especially in times of industrial depression.

We looked abroad, and saw the good fruit of care for and attention to the problem of the condition of the people, in the case especi- ally of our great neighbours the Germans; and we said, and none too soon, the good old happy-go-lucky, muddle-along methold won't do any longer. It's all very well to sing raucous choruses about "The Boys of the Bulldog Breed"; but there are lots of quar- ters in which that breed stands sorely in need of care and attention.

So we have set ourselves to build up the British Constitution at a moment, curiously enough, when, in another sense, our oppo- nents are furiously denouncing us as evillS•- disposed persons anxious enougli to destroy that Constitution! THE NEED FOR THE ACT.

Now, in our survey of the social condition of the people, amidst a welter of indifference and carelessness, a most reassuring feature presents itself. We see that large bodies of working men and women have banded them- selves together voluntarily through friendly society and trade union to make some pro- vision for the rainy day. That is excellent ; and if the spirit which inspires these good piople were universal amongst our industrial population there would have been no neces- sity for a National Insurance Act, for a " revolt " of the doctors, or for the " servant tax " agitation. Neither would delicately- reared ladies of quality go in danger of being poisoned by stamp-licking. But that spirit does not pervade the whole field; it operates only over about half, and unfortunately the other half, generally speak- ing, represents members of the community who need the protection of insurance most of all. So we have put our hands to the task of making the latter half do under compulsion that which the former has done voluntarily— that is all. Or not quite, because we are pro- pcsing to come to the assistance of both with very substantial State subventions.

div.head: lIOW IT WILL BE WORKED.
div.p: lIOW IT WILL BE WORKED.

Very good! In this great scheme of deve- loping more widely the habit of making provision for the rainy day our course is clear. We must, as far as possible, work through existing organisations. There they are on the ground; they have bought expert- ;Jim Through them we can most economic- ally and anti-bureaucratically conduct our compulsory extension operations. So, for the purposes of Part I. of the Act, we invite all sorts of existing thrift societies to conform to the regulations necessary for " approval." We compel everybody between sixteen and seventy years of age, if employed and if earn- ing less than £l6O a year, to insure against sickness and disablement b, joining or con- tinuing in an " approved' society. Each person thus compulsorily insured will make a weekly contribution; the employer will con- tribute; the State will contribute. Later articles will give you full details of these con- tributions, and how they will be made. Then, subject to clue safeguards for the proper application of the money, the " approved, ' societies will, conjointly with admirably con- stituted local Insurance Committees, and with the advice and assistance of a powerfully con stituted Insurance Commission at the centre, dispense the benefits which these threefold contributions will make possible. Here, again, later articles will set out these benefits in detail. Obvibusly they must be on a more generous scale than any friendly society that desired to remain solvent can offer, because, of course, such society has had no subvention from employer or State wherewith to augment its members' subscriptions. ITS INSURANCE BENEFITS.

But more! To start this scheme we I.me imported a striking and novel feature. WE have put full insurance reserve values behind every life from twenty-one (and in some cases from sixteen) to fifty; and further, stb- stantial reserve values behind every !de from fifty to sixty-five. This has made it possible to give the same benefits for 4d. a week con- tributed by the man who is fifty at the corn mencement of the Act as for 4d. a week contributed by the man who is twenty-one at the commencement of the Act. Now nc friendly society has been able to do this. In- deed, if you had reached fifty without insur- ing before the Act was passed, the probability is that no friendly society would entertain you as an insurable person ea all. You will ask how we have been able to de this. Simply by fixing a scale of benefit lower than 9d. would produce for the young person insuring at sixteen higher than 9d. would produce for the older amongst the corn- pulsorily insured persons. Yes! But once this thing is started all new entrants will come •in at sixteen. They will build up their own insurance reserve values as they gc along. Gradually, therefore, we shall wipe out the liability with which we are burdened on account of these, older lives. What thenl Why, money will be set free, and the scale of possible benefits will be proportionately en- hanced. _ .

So far I have been dealing with the case of the person who is able to get into an tip. Proved society. But there are those whose health record is such tint* no friendly society has accepted them; no approved society will take them. Their insurance under this Act will be effected through the Post Office. The details of the scheme as it affects the Post Office depositor will be set forth fully by latet writers.

Now there it is—the greatest and most generous scheme of State intervention into the condition of the people ever attempted in this or any other country. It may not achieve everything the most ardent amongst us may hope. Certain sections of the com- munity may slip through the meshes of the net which, in their own and the national inte- rest, we have thrown over them. But this is certain. In a few years from now the num- ber of those who have acquired the habit of making provision for the rainy day will have been doubled. That will represent one of the greatest social reforms ever accomplished. For the rest, if we fall short of complete suc- cess with the casually employed, the unskilled labourer who wanders from one field of occu- pation to another, the man in and out of odd jobs, and the camp follower of organised in- dustrialism, so be it. Try again. GROUNDLESS APPREHENSIONS.

As a man representing a working-class constituency, I do not deny that many of my poorest friends have their apprehensions. In some cases these are sincere, though, as time will show, unnecessary and groundless. You have only to study what the poorest-paid German operative is doing to-day to see what can be done in the way of weekly contribu- tions towards a scheme of this sort. But in many cases those apprehensions have been manufactured and exploited for purely parti• 'san purposes. The fact is—and it would be fatuous not to recognise it—there is a type of political partisan who only examines the pro- posals of his opponents for the purposes of seeing how best he may denounce them. That type has literally revelled in the opening this. Act has given him. He has thrown every difficulty—real and imaginary—on to the largest screen, in the highest light, and to an accompaniment of the most disquieting music. Its splendid benefits he has curtly dismissed. And, by inference at any rate, he has tried to make poor people believe how much better the thing would have been done if he had been left to do it. Yes, I know! If he had been left to do it we should all have been mouldering in our graves before ever he had made a start! And the amusing thing is this. Your 1)011. tical dog-in-the-manger is always the first to come and fawn upon you and ask yoor grate- rennanition for services rendered .when
he snarled at has become a nrst• class- success.

So it will be here. Before long all the poli- tical dogs-in-the-mangers will be wagging their tails and barking with ostentatious de- light at the help they gave- the poor people to make tlis great and beneficent Act an accomplished fact. The aim of this ccries of articles will be to see that the people know and know fully the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth about this great scheme. If this end be attained, those who axe re- sponsible for it—and the people may be trusted to discriminate accurately upon that point—may await the verdict with the most complete equanimity.
LVext week's article will be contributed by Mr. L. Chiozza Money, M.P.]

The matter gave rise to ccnsiderable diecuzsion at the monthly meeting of the committee on Monday evening. Councillor H Roberts presided and there were also present :—Mr A J Jolley (deputy- chairman), Alderman A Bennett, Councillors 'l' &litles, .1 Pemberton, W H Be!lien, J T Locker, C Jackson ' Holmes, W J Wilson, W H J Jenkins, J Dickenson, Revs Canon Morley Stevenson, .1 Davies and Neville Wilson, Messrs It T Fairclottgh, C N Parker, N Plinston, H Kingdon, J Chrimes, 0 Walker, J Upson, J Moore Murray (director of education), and It B Roberts (assistant director). div.head: WRECK OF THE P. & 0. OCEANA.
div.p: THE WRECK OF THE P. & 0. OCEANA.

Early on Saturday mornina the P. and 0. liner Oceana, which left Tilbury on Friday for Bombay, was run into and sunk by a German barque off Eastbourne. The crew and passengers were rescued by boats, but one was swamped, and several lives were lost. There was £750,000 in specie on board. The

Alderman BENNETT thought the Committee were making a somewhat serious mistake. If they debarred a large propor- tion of the qualified members of that recognized society from competing, they would be stultifying themselves and failing to secure the best results. The Rev JAMES DAVIES asked who was to be the assessor with respect to the designs to be sent in. Canon STEVENSON replied that the representations were not of course made with the sugration that the children should be kept at school ; all the Committee bad done was to ask the Board for further help. The Board of Education have writtea sanctioning, as an experimental measure, the proposed arrangements for the establishment of a school dental clinic. div.head: ZOUTE, NEAR OSTEND.
div.p: THE ZOUTE, NEAR OSTEND.

The seaside resort called The Zoute is, in realily, an extension of Knock° towards the North-east, and com- prising all the dunes from there to the Dutch frontier. The Zoute Co., (Compagnie Immobilibre Le Zoute) in creating this new part, has done its utmost to respect the natural beauties of this wild and yet smiling land so that visitors enjoy the pleasures of the seashore as well as delightiul walks over the downs and through the woods. Truly nature is kind and spoils this little corner of Belgium, as far as climate is concerned ; nowhere does It, rain less! Scarcely 60 centimeters fall in 12 menthe, whereas the raingauge in Brussels indicates 73 ! One must go to the shores of the Mediterranean, to Il36res, Perpignan or Barcelona, to find any part where there are fewer rainy days than at the Zoute. Twelve years of close observation, show an average of 131 wet days at Knocke,whilst the Royal Observatory establishes the record of 118 in Brussels. Toulouse In the South of France, has 140 rainy days. This invaluable advantage to all who come to the cent to renew their strength in its fresh sea-breezes and the life-giving atmosphere of its dunes, attracts a great many vititors, who find the Zoute an unique ceLtre for 01er210119.

AN APPEAL TO THE BOARD OF EDUCATION.

The School Management Committee have bad under cone ideration the injurious effect upon the work in the public elementary schools of the exclusion of so large a cumber of children from school attendance through infectious and cmttagious diseases. It was decided to make representations to the Board of Education upon the matter (more especially from the point of view that the faithful fulfilment of their du: ies in this matter both by the committee end their efficers results in educational and fleancial loss) in the hope that the Board may see their way to make some provision which will minimise at least some part of the financial loss." Canon STEVENSON said the excellent way in whioh the medical officer and his helpers were carrying out the Act for the medical inspection of children resulted in the withdrawal from school of a large number of scholars and the decrease in attendances brought about a serious diminution of grant. div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The General Upset.—At the best, it will be some time before the n irmal condition of commercial and industrial life is resumed after the coal strike, and it will be much the same as regards the effect upon the social world. The stoppage has caused the King and Queen to give up, for this year, their projected foreign visit, and several engag smelts involving travel by rail or by sea, have been either postponed or abandoned. Their Majesties have so ninny home engagements for the slimmer and autumn months, thst the spring alone was available for the contempla at official visit to Paris and other capitils of Eurt pe. The disturbed outlook has also seriouvly interfered with the Easter holiday arrangements of the general public. To the übiquitous inquiry " What are you going to do at Easter?" the general reply has been" must wait and see." Arrangements in numberless cases have to he made beforehand, and these have been diffi- cult in vfew of doubtful traveliing facilities. The London sccial season has also suffered. Wealthy hostesses have been relactant to enter upon a round of entertainments at a time of so much distress among the industrial classes. That seems natural, although it is perhaps a little illogical, seeing that it is neither good for trade nr for thousands who are dependent on the lavish expenditure of the West Eod of London. The Livery Companies of London.—There have been but few instances of women being enrolled as members of the Livery Companies of ths City of London. The Gardeners Company, which was incorporated in 1605, and is roe of the oldest of the City Livery Comp lilies, has a1wa7,13 admitted lady app-en ices, but they have been few and far between. The Fishmongers' Company have three ladies on their roll, and the fanmakers one— the Marchionrss of Bristol in recognition of the interest she h^s taken in the art end history of fanmaking. The Linmakers have recently admitted two girl apprentices, a new departure in the reeulaions of this company. Apprenticeship lasts for seven years, during which time the apprentices may not frequent taverns, or marry without the consent of the Company. As regards the majority of the guilds, the old-time regulations and privileges never contemplated the admission of women, but now that a fresh start has been made, it is possible that women may invade these ancient and sacred haunts of masculinity. The Revolution in the World of Dress.—Although the powers that be have ordained that changes shall be introduced into every department of women's dress, these are not of a revolutionary nature, and many of last rear's dres-es, that are still in good condition will require only minor modifications t 3 bring them up-to- date. For instance a plain evening gown will lend itself admirably to the draperies of the moment, or to a tunic of ninon, of plain or embroidered net, or of any transparent niaterial. The colour may be the same as the dress, black, or any contrasting or harmonising I shade may be chosen. The draperies should start from the waist, be brought round to within a few inches of the hem, but not touch the hips, as the slender effect must be maintained, and the more one-sided their arrangement the more fashionable will be the dress. The materials for spring wear—with the possibilities of draperies in the near future—are exquisitely supple soft and clinging. Coats and Skirts.—Every year the tailor-made suit gains in popularity, and this season's attractive models will certainl; add to the number of its admirers. Coats are still moderately short, although the length is some- what a matter cf individual taste. Models prepared for young girls ahow quite short coats, those for their elders being generally longer—sllm and slender women I looking well in either. The tailor-made is trimmed this season much more than last, and the trimming— usually covered cord, buttons, braid or motifs—is placed on skirts as well as coats. The Long Spring Coat.—A very sensible modern fashion is the long spring or race coat, that takes the place of the long fur garment, and considerately covers up the deficiencies of gowns that have done duty dnring the winter. The Directoire in satin, brocade,or silk, is the most popular style. There is also the Polonaise coat with sweeping lines, and the Mother Ifubbard, a full clock rather than a coat, with gauging on ,he shoulders, and a deep lane collar or embroidered yoke. In fire cloth, braided to match, the long spring coat is a desirable garment, for theatre, or concert wear,whilst for cold days there are smart models in reversible cloths in all the new colours. Some New Shades.—Blues are maintaining their position, and a revival to be noted is the old-time rale blue,beloved of our mothers,in which there is not a sus- picion of turquoise ;it is just that soft tone that makes a grey eye look blue, and blue eye take a deeper shade. Lettuce green is a charming spring colour effectively used for cuffs, revers, and collars of tailored suits in ecru tints. Tailors are shewing models for early spring wear in sober greens, more especially the new seaweed shades. Greys, too, deserve mentiontand include mole- skin hues, lavenders, and all mineral neutrals. Sahara,or sand of Egypt, is a new name for putty shades, ranging from palest t4O to golden brown. The latter colour is not only shot with mauve, blue, green and rose, to form the chameleon or changing tints, but is seen in plAti shades and in stripes. Two lovely and well-wearing hues in brown are noisetta and tortoise-shell. Anemone purple is another rich shade, and malachite green is cool-looking and restful to the eye. Stripes Again.—Every description of dress material evinces the continued popularity of stripes, even heavy cloths, tweeds end serve, have prayed unable to resist the vogue, and both tailors and dressmakers rise giving stripes the preference over every optherpattern.stripes. Tsaptof et tat Spotted foulards, voiles, and later on all cotton goods, will have broad spaced out, composite, or in foulards—mostly white spots on coloured grounds, will be seen also, and a novelty in this connection will be the stripe-bordered foulards and muslin s. Concerning Bouquets.—" Posy " bouquets—closely trhnieedarsbty ourur t _g rbaanvdemeontib beyresd, and t rrneusecmh binlinegvidthenoscee acta a brief revival. Composed ohs variety of small flowers closely pricked, the " posy " has proved weighty and somewhat unweildy, and certainly it in no way approaches the "shower bouquet from on artistic point of view.

div.p: Stockton Heath.

FUNERAL OF MRS. SARAH BROADV.—The funeral took place at St. Thomas' Churchyard on Sunday 'afternoon of the late Mrs. Sarah Broady, the wife of Mr. Henry Broady, of Mountain Farm, Grappenhall. Mrs Broady. who was a daughter of the late Mr T Spencer, of Church Farm, Stockton Heath, died on the 11th inst., at the age of forty-seven years. The Revs J Collins and H V Pigot officiated. ~The mourners included Mr Henry Broady (husband), Messrs H and F Broady (sons), J Starkey, H A Unsworth and J Woods (brothers-in-law), Alfred Broady, Albert Broady, Tom Broady, Fred Broady, F Pearson, William Mclntyre, le Timperley, James Carter, Joseph Broady, Clubley, W Ford, J H Mclntyre, J Shepherd, J Parkes, J Ditchfield, W Bennion, F Hughes, Plumb, J Maxfield, Burnage, Rigby, CII Hughes and J S and II Hughes. div.head: Lymm.
div.p: Lymm.

LncTCRE AT THE GRAMMAR SCHOOL.—Ou Saturday night last a lecture on "Church History" was delivered at the Grammar School by the Rev. R. P. NVetherhead. Limelight views manipulated by Mr. C. Moss were used to illustrate the lecture.

CHRISTIAN ENDEAVOUR ANNIVERSARY.—The Young People's Societies of Christian Endeavour in connec- tion with the Primitive Methodist Church cele- brated their anniversary on Sunday and Monday last. There were good attendances at all the services. The Rev. S. R. Woodall, of Hol'lnwood, Oldham, a former minister of the Lymm Circuit, preached two earnest sermons on Sunday. The evening service being further enriched by the singing of Miss Greta Welford, of West Kirby. Mr Woodall &livered a suitable address at the meeting presided over by Mr T Muss, the president, on M3nday night. COIL STRIKE.—Up to the present our District Council have not issued notice of any curtailment in the supply of gas for lighting and other dothestio pur- poses, but consumers generally would be acting in their own interests, and at the same time assisting the Gas Department, in prolonging the period of full supply, by economising in every possible way. It is with feelings of sincere regret that we have to recard the felling of some fine trees in the Elollow,for the purpose of supplying the local water works with fuel for the pumping machinery. This is, of course, a private m Atter in which we have no voice, but we do not like to part with old friends, even though they be " wooden " ones. It is with quite different feelings that we observe numbers of workmen wending their homeward way on the edge of dark, laden with faggots to supplement the coal deficiency. Children too, singly and in groups:seem to meet with considerable success in their quest of firing, though it would perhaps be indiscreet to enquire the source of their various capture.. Possibly the farmers could throw some light on the subject, as they are at present giving special attention to roadside fences. We may say in passing, and judging from the multifarous and not always agreeable odours frequently distributed through the atmosphere, that coal and wood are not the only combustibles at present being used for heating purposes in some of the cottages.

. • CONGREGATIONAL CHOIR SOclAt,—On Wednesday night the Congregational choir held a social evening in the schoolroom which was well patronised. Mr Thomas in taking the chair stated that he regretted having to fill the position which should have been occupied by Mr J D B Smith who had unfortunately been detained in Liverpool. A song by seven boys and girls entitled "Welcome " appropriately opened the programme. Mr Massey, of Knutsford gave a recitation called " The social scale." Mr Douglas Holt came next with a solo. A duet, ' Keys of Heaven," sung by Mrs Lewis and Mr J Hewitt, embellished with humorous actions, brought forth a hearty demand for more, which request was kindly given. Mr Massey gave another recitation " Kissing Cup's Race," the climax of which gave ample evidence of his good elocutionary powers and merited the generous applause given him. The succeeding item was a well-rendered action song, " Cups of tea," by five girls. Mr C Leather sang The sea is England's glory." Six boys then sang " Ring, ring de banjo," the chores being accompanied with playing on bones. Refreshments were dispensed by the choir members. Mr Massey sang a rolliaking song of good advice entitled " Keep your houses clean," the audience joining in the chorus ; needless perhaps, to mention that this item was encored. A duet by Miss Boond and Mr Sumner was also encored. Mr. Massey's last contribution wes a recitation called "Tao Duke and the stone.' The popular sketch " Handy Andy " brought the programme to a close. The various parts were well sustained by Miss Evans, and Messrs D Holt, Sumner, .1 Hewitt, and C Leather. Mrs Gotobed and Mr. Leather officiated as accompanists. Votes of thanks to the workers were proposed by Mr Bell, seconded by Mr. Willan and carried with acclamation. The singing of the National Anthem terminlted the social, PETTY SESSIONS.

PERSISTENT CRUELTY.—AmeIia Bra zendale, Islington- street, Altrincham, summoned her husband, George Brazendale, 6, Brookfield Cottages, Lymm, for persistent cruelty.—Complainant said her husband had repeatedly struck her and was like a madman, if anyone said any- thing to him. He had seized her by the throat and struck her in the face. in consequence of his treat- ment, she bad had to leave him. Corroborative evidence was given by the daughters, Bertha and Martha, the latter of whom stated that defendant had hit her in the face on one occasion. Complainant also stated that on three occasions her husband bad only given her 'ls. 6d. at the week-ends.—Defendant denied that be had been guilty of cnielty and said his wife had run him in for debt without saying a word to him about it. He had given her sufficient money. Other evidence was given for both sides and a separation order with 10a. per week alimony was granted. div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
MR. J. DILLON AT EARLESTOWN. THE COLONIES AND HOME RULE.

Mr J. Dillon, M.P., on Saturday night, addressing a meeting at Earlestown, said when the Home Rule Bill was introduced there would come from all corners of the earth expressions of sympathy and demands that the Government should pass the bill into law. He ventured to say there was not a s;ngle British colony that would not send to the Imperial Parliament a strong demand for the granting of Home Rule. Every one of the great dominions knew that if they had been den;ell Home Rule they would not be loyal to Great Britain to-day, but on the contrary would have long ago snapped the bond of union and declared them- selves independent. They appreciated the effects of liberty. In other da3 s Ireland was, according to the Unionists, a poverty-striken, disorderly country, and was not fit for Home Rule. Now the country was orderly and prosparons and did not want Home Rule. (Laughter.) The Unionists of Ireland had an English. man to govern them. and they were not content under Mr. Birrell's nee. The only thing that would content them was a ruler like Mr. Balfour. Their modest idea was that the people should submit to Tory rule for ever. The Orangemen with their recent threats of violence had disgraced their city, exposed themselves to the charge of being rowdies, and advertised Mr. Churchill's speech to the four corners of the world. SHOP ASSISTANTS AND LABOUR POLITICS.

div.head: SPEECH BY MR. J. A. SEDDON.
div.p: SPEECH BY MR. J. A. SEDDON.

A meeting of the shop assistsnts and clerks, called by the trade unions interested in their organisation, was held In the Milton Hall, Deaosgate' on Sunday night. Mr .1 Hat iswort h, of the Co-operative Employees' Union, presided. There was a large attendance. . .

J A Seddon, who formerly represented the Newton division as a Labour member, referring to the Shops Act, said it was only fair they should recognise that Mr Churchill, when he was at the Home Office, did far more than many IMinisters would have done to get the original bill through Parliament, and that if it had not been for his pertinacity they would not have got even what they had. The Act as passed was nothing much to crow over, but by giving the shop assistant a statutory right to a weekly ball-holiday and by scheduling the meal times established two most valuable principles. If the sliop assistants of Manchester were not very careful, however they would have the Act weakened by the relay system, under which the shops would remain open and the assistants would take their half-day in rotation. Mr Seddon, speaking on the Insurance Act, strongly urged all shop assistants and clerks to choose a trade union when entering an approved society. In the Shop Assistants' Union, owing to the comparatively small cost of the sickness benefits, they anticipated a large surplus under the Act, and they proposed to offer members additional benefits. Speaking of the necessity for orgau:sation, :4r. Seddon said he believed labour was going to have its greatest battle before long. The capitalists were concentrating. They had an illustration of what one group could do to help other groups in the stoppage of so many trains during the coal strike. There was no necessity for the stoppage, and the railway companies were inconveniencing the public deliberately with the idea of creating feeling against the trade unions. Mr. J. If. Pearce, of the National Union of Clerks, also addressed the meeting.

div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

FREE MEALS FOR 2,C0) SCHOOL CHILDREN. At especially convened meeting f the Widnes Educa- tion Authority, in the Town Hall, on Wednesday, a resolution proposing to put into operation the Educa- tion (Provision of Meals) Act was carried. The Mayor (Alderman F Neil) who presided, skid something like 1,000 heads of families were out of work, and in consequence there was destitution among the children. Under the Act they could only look after children five days a week, so that to look after them over the week-end funds would have to he voluntarily. Mr Calvert suggested that the rate could be increased to Id. Mr Craik (the deputy town clerk) said the maximum allowed under the Act was The Mayor had invited the co-operation of the teschers, and it was proposed to give the children a good breakfast and dinner. To guard against imposi- tion they would work hand in hand with the Board of Guardians.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

Of the excellent and varied programme submitted at the Hippodrome this week, much of a praiseworthy nature could be said for it is one of those rare treats, an entertainment without a single blemish all through' What a pleasure it was to listen ta the harmonious renditions by the .Comedy Meisters, a troupe of four men gifted with exceptionally good voices, which they use to advantage in many popular songs. A fair amount of humour is kept up by two of the company and the turn is repeatedly called upon for encores. A neat and clever acrobatic turn is that provided by the Martelloni family, four ladies and a gentleman who, during the time they are on the stage get through a series of dangerous and clever tricks with remarkable swiftness and grace. Jack Clevoner shows himself to be a thorough master of the concertina and plays many selections and airs in a pleasing and humorous manner. Mr. Irve Hayman and Little Nora Williams appear with succcess in a sketch " Christmas Eve " in which the burglar is reformed by the innocent chatter and harmless actions of the child. " Not a crook " is the title given to the breezy racing act by Phil Rees stable lads aid is indeed a success There are seven youngsters who sing and dance in a very clever and entertaining manner and the audience are not slow to appreciate. John Weil mystifies and amuses the audience with a large number of sleight of hand tricks which Ire performs with really pheno- menal expertru ss He has a pleasing style and is one of the cleverest artistes of this kind we have had in Warrington for some time.
"MIK."
The famous thought-reading dog who will make his first appearance in Warrington at the Hippodrome next week. " Mik "is said to represent the last word in canine intelligence and animal training.

div.head: DEATH TRAP.
div.p: A DEATH TRAP.
CHILD DROWNED IN SANKEY BROOK.

An inquiry was conducted at the Coroner's Court on Tuesday by Mr. S. Brighouse, concerning the death of Elizabeth Deakin, aged six years, daughter of llerbett Deakin, 2, Ernest-street. Annie Deakin, the mother said, she last saw her daughter alive at 5,30 on Monday evening. At (115 pm. she heard she bad fallen into the Sankev Brook and the body was recovered by the Warrington Grappling Corps. Evelyn Kelly said Elizabeth Deakin walked down the hill and slipped into the brook.—Frederick Dutton, the vlce-c3ptalll of the Grappling Corps, said the place was 4sa proper death-trap." and should be fenced off.—lt icis mentioned by a juryman that the attention of the owners had been drawn to the place on the occasion of a similar fatality, and Mr Brighouse asked the jury to leave the matter with him, and he would go and visit the spot and endeavour to get. the owners to remove the danger. A verdict of "Accidental duel" was retuned.

div.head: STRIKE.
div.p: THE STRIKE.
THE LOSS OF WAGES.
Interesting Figures at Town's Meeting.
"NO ACUTE DISTRESS."

There was a large and representative attendance at the meeting convened by the Mayor and held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall on Monday after- noon to consider what steps (if any) should be taken to relieve distress caused by the strike. His worship pre- sided and in opening the proceedings said the meeting had been called to ascertain whether any distress existed and, so far as he had been able to ascertain, he was pleased to think it was not yet abnormal. The TOWN CLERK read several letters of apology for non-attendance. Mr F W Monks wrote that it had been deemed advisable to start a relief kitchen in Messrs. Monks, Hall siul Company's works, and that it had been working satisfactorily since Saturday. One good meal a day would be provided for workmen employed by the firm, together with their wives and children. Children attending school would be supplied only on Saturday and Sunday so as not to clash with what was being done by the Education Committee. Mr. Robert Pierpoint wrote : It is not the first time in my experience that the works io Warrington have had to be closed or put on short time through want of coal in consequence of a coal strike. That some measures will have to he taken under your auspices for the relief of the inevitable distress is, I fear, certain. If thou:, circumstances arise, I beg you to call upon me for a subscripton of £5 a week for four weeks from the date of the relief fund, if such relief has, unhappily, to continue so long. My wife asks me to say that she desires to contribute £2 per week for the same time. Although we do not not now live in Warrington, we cannot free ourselves from our interest in and affection for the old town. Mr. Harold Smith, M.P., telegraphed to the Town Clerk desiring to associate himself with the object of the meeting and to co-operate with the Mayor in any decision which the meeting adopted. He was sure the Mayor would have a ready response to any appeal he might make. The MAYOR said there was a small balance of £66 103 4d from the last Mayor's relief fund in 1969-10. He thought it would be a good thing if each firm laid itself out to relieve its own employes. That would simplify the relief measures very materially and prevent over-lapping. Mr. J. J. BLECKLY, after recalling his asscciation with the relief efforts during the cotton famine of 1860, said his own opinion was that at the present time there was little or no acute distress. If other people would furnish the information that his firm had been ascertaining, as to oho was really short and who was well supplied, it would be a great advantage to start with. For the last full week's work on the second of March the wages of their company amounted to £1,071 ; Rylands Brothers to £2,116 ; last week (a short week) the wages at Messrs. Pearson and Knowles amounted to £2,233, and at Messrs Rylands Bros. £1,830. The whole amount from the united concern was £6,305 while in full work, and £3,976 whiie on abort time, so that the deficiency upon the gross total of £6,304 was £2,328. But that only answered part of the question. That money was not equally distributed. There were many cases amongst the workmen of urgent necessity, although their mates were well supplied with funds, and if they had not at the present moment that urgent necessity, it was coming, and it would come on with increasing intensity as time went on. At the end of the week they would feel the first pull upon them, the next week the tecessity would be great, and the week after it might be appalling. It was, therefore, wise to provide a nucleus. (Hear, hear.) The first step to take was to appoint a new committee. That was not a case for panic legislation, but for steady preparation, but if they appointev a strong committee to go into details they would be prepared for an emergency as it arose. He ventured to differ from the suggestion which had been made that each firm should apply to their own workmen the assistance they required. That would be frittering away and reducing the capability of the good that could be done which, with a larger administration, could be more economical. (Hear, hear.) The fund must be recog- nized as not for general purposes, but as specifically ear- marked for this particular emergency. If they did not do that they would impoverish all the ordinary charitable insitutions of the town, which would prove to be most mischievous. This was not the time for large donations and a general distribution. (Hear, hear.) If the strike continued—and no man in that room could tell whether it would last one, three, or 30 weeks, and he had had to do with strikes—they would require economy in the first instance [and a business-like distribution upon proper terms, so that the right men could get the right assistance. If they gave big donations and frittered away their funds it would be worse for them. Let them adequately provide their part week by week, and not put down large sums to be squandered unnecessarily. (Hear' hear). Mr A Bo I TONILEY (Clerk to the Board of Guardians) said that up to that morning the number of applicants for relief from persons directly affected by the strike was 63, relating to 310 persons. They had not received as many applications as they bad expected—not nearly as many as they had during the railway strike—but every day they expected a large nuniser of applications to come in. The relieving officers were dealing with the oases. A committee should be formed immediately as there were already many on the verge of starvatiou. They had not had many cases from the Sankey district,' nearly all were from the Bewsey district, and most of the men had been employed at the forges. Mr 3 1 BLECKLEY then moved a resolution :—"That a committee be appointed to consider and carry into effect means for relieving the distress among the poor caused by the coal strike, the committee to have power to add to their number."

Captain CROSFIELD seconded the resolution. He intimated that forttinately Messrs. Crosfleld and Sons had not found it necessary to dismiss any men and the works could be kept running for another few weeks. He regarded the suggestion that the firms should look after their own workers as a very sound one. If the strite continued it was the intention of Messrs. Crosfleld to advance their workmen about 10s. per week each to tide them over any time of distress and to obtain repayment when full work was resumed. He thought that was a more desirable system to follow than to distribute relief wholesale and run the risk of patipsrising people. The Rev, W. BRACECAMP said that in St. Paul's parish there was absolutely no need, except as regarded the children, for any distribution of relief. The municipal authorities, through the Education Committee, had power to spend a certain amount and if the children were fed he thought there would not be any necessity at present for a relief fund. " I have been told on good authority that the places of amusement in Warrington have simply been packed from end to end the whole of this last week," he remarked, "and I think it will be a great mistake if it goes ont to the public that we are starting a relief fund at the present time." He had only had two applications for assistance in consequence of the strike during the past fortnight, and he urged that action should be delayed. Otherwise they would simply be inundated with applications and their other work would be crippled and hindered in many wet's. Councillor H ROBERTS said he could not agree with Mr Bracecamp. It was no use locking the stable door after the horse had been stolen, and the resolution was simply taking time by the forelock and making provi- ston in case it was found necessary. As a matter of prudence, there was no getting away from the fact that if the strike continued the number of men out of employment would gradually increase and poverty would be intensified. He did not attach much import- ance to the statement that the places of amusement had been packed. The men out of work had to go some- where, and it was better that they should go there than to some places one could mention. He did not think they could afford to throw stones at the working men in Matters of that kind. The RECTOR said there was some truth in what Mr Bracecamp had said regarding the comparatively small amount of distress prevailing. lie knew of but few cases, and very few applications had been made to him. At the same time there was great wisdom in Mr Bleckly's proposition that they should take time by the forelock and make preparation for what would probably come upon them. Councillor ASHCROFT said his impressions were, after constantly visiting the various parts of the district, that there was a large number of cases of distress at present in the St. Austin's mil Bewsey Wards. The Rev. WM. COOPER said he had made inquiry among his own people, and so far there was no need for anxiety, but if the strike should•continue there wculd be some urgent need for a fund. The better course was to be prepared. Mr. I3oTromLei said the relieving officers reported that if something was not done before the end of the week there were many cases, in which families would be practically stsiving. The MAYOR said the situation seemed to be that so far no great amount of distress was manifest, but it seemed probable, if the strike was prolonged, that the pinch would begin to be felt. Harm might be done by being too ready to give relief, but it was wise that they should be prepared to move at the right moment. A member of the audience who described himself as a workingman declared that there was much dietress in the Bewsey district, " There are, I believe" he said "many honest men with families who do not know whereto get their tea from this afternoon." Mr. Bleckly's motion was carried unanimously, and a large committee, ex-officio, the clergy and ministers, the secretary to thel), the secretary to the Trades and Labour Guild of Help, consisting of the Mayor, as chairman Council, representative from the various works affected by the strike, members of the Board of Guardians and others,was elected with power to form an executive for . the distribution of relief should it be found necessary to open a fund,
No Immediate Need.

A meeting of the Executjue Committee was held on Tuesday evening, at the Town liall,the Mayor presiding over a good attendance. Delegates front the principal works of the town were present. From information supplied by the delegates as to the conditions of employment in the different works, and of the generous help given in several of them to those out of employ- mont,it %%as felt that there was no immediate necessity to rnise a public fund. It was, !therefore, unanimously decided to adjourn the meeting sine die, but it was uneerstood that the Mayor would convene another meeting if necessity arose.

div.head: FEEDING OF CHILDREN. EDUCATION COMMITTEE PREPARED TO DEAL WITH 800 CASES.
div.p: THE FEEDING OF CHILDREN. EDUCATION COMMITTEE PREPARED TO DEAL WITH 800 CASES.

The question of the arrangements which are being made by the education authority to provide meals for necessitious children during the strike was raised at the meeting of the Education Committee on Monday even- ing by Mr. C. E. Parker. He said he had no doubt that the matter was already in hand but, as the question would probably become a very serious one, it V 7119 desirable that the committee should know what steps were being taken. Mr.E. PLINsToS, chairman of the School Attend- ance Committee, said that the committee were quite prepared to deal with the question as soon as it became urgent. The Director had informed him that up to that day there had not been any increase in the number of names submitted by the teachers. It was anticipated that if the dispute con- tinued there must he at a very early date a number of children who would be suffering privation. The com- mittee were prepared, in case of emergency, to deal with a substantial Increase in the demand for feeding. but if that demand became abnormal other metbods would have to be adopted, because the amount allowed out of the rates would not permit them to deal with the difficulties which might arise a fortnight hence. Councillor Brum:, stated that he had visited the place where the meals ware provided that morning. All the children seemed healthy. There were two more partaking of the food than were provided for last week but there were not so many as a month ago. There were 30 cases a month ago ; 21 last week ; and 20 this week.
The CiIAIRMAN : If there is an increase of acute distress you will be prepared to deal with it ? Mr PuNsTos : At once.

Mr. UPSON said there seemed to be some little doubt amongst the teachers as to whether they were at liberty to report cases of children whom they knew to be suffering from want of food for immediate relief, or whether they ought to wait for the cases to be medically examined first. He understood, however, that it was not necessary to wait for the medical examination. The CH AIRM AN : That is so.

Mr. PLINSTON remarked that it was suggested that teachers should report first and then the cases should be medically examined afterwards. Everyone would admit that in face of what was before them the fact that the teachers sent in the names was quite sufll3ient. The authority would then immediately deal with the cases where the necessity of feeding was apparent. The CHAIRMAN: Feed first and e xamine afterwards. In reply to Mr. Kixu DON. the CHAIRMAN stated that the maximum available for the feeling of necessitous children was a halfpenny rate of one year, and that would produce bete een £lOO and £5OO. The DIRECTOR said h 3 spent the greater part of Thursday and Friday making investigations and it was pleasing to say that with the exception of one school, the teachers load not noticed any increase of oases nor had there been any applicatioss from the parents. As long as the numbers did not Exceed a reasonable limit—they could deal with between COO and 800 cases. there was no cause for uneasiness, but if the numbers went beyond the figures mdmtioned it would be necessary to consider whether breakfast, dinner and tea or dinner only should be provided. A number of teachers had already willingly volunteered to do any extra work that might be necessary. The only thing necessary would be the making of arrangements for the transport of the food to the schools, and that could be dons.

_ Mr KINGDON: If we spend all the money on feeding necessitous children during the coal strike will it be possible to deal with the ordinary cases, caused by unemployment, towards the end of the year? The DIRECTOR : Another financial year starts on April Ist. The CIIAIR3IAN said there seemed no doubt that if any serious and abnormal condition of affairs arose consequent upon the coal strike, special means would have to be found for dealing with it, but for the moment they were in a position to deal with anything like an ordinary increase such as was anticipated under present conditions. div.head: MORE RIOTOUS SCENES NEAR EARLESTOWN.
div.p: MORE RIOTOUS SCENES NEAR EARLESTOWN.
POLICE COURT SEQUEL AT !ARRINGTON.

------- There were riotous scenes at Collins Green, near Earlestown, on Tuesday, resulting in baton charges by the police and the arrest of three youths who are alleged to have takan an active part in the disturbance. The crowd began to gather about eleven o'clock in the morning, but the London and North-Western main line which leads to Bold Colliery was found to be well guarded with police. In view of the menacing attitude of several hundred would-be coal pickers from St. Helens and Earlestown, extra men had been arriving at Collins Green from different parts of the country dur- leg the preceding twenty-four hours, and there was, luckily for the colliery people, an ample force to deal with the emergency. Soon after noon the police noticed that the rowdy element had collected stones and macadam into heaps on the road outside the colliery yard at Collins Green, and it was decided to clear the road. A charge was made and the crowd driven back towards St. Helens. The rioters then began to send occasional shots into the colliery yard by means of slings fired from long range. Several police were hit, but not seriously. About three o'clock in the afternoon the rioter; who were led by several vengeful cudgellers, decided on tactical movements, and simultaneously made attacks from two different sides of the colliery premises. The police, however, charged home with their batons time after time, ad blows were given and received on both sides, the victory resting with the police. Several other skirmishes followed, but as the crowd would not leave, the mounted police were summoned from Prescot and piloted to the colliery by a constable on a bicycle. Between five and six o'clock the melee was becoming general, and the police had their hands very full. The four mounted officers dashed into the fray about a quarter to six, and scattered the crowd in all directions POLICE COURT PROCEEDINGS. A sequel to the riots was heard at the Warrington County Sessions, on Wednesday, when three youths, named John Crawford, James Gibson, and William Hancock, residing at Parr, were charged with riotously assembling to disturb the peace. Sergeant Smith, of the County Constabulary detailed the nature of the offence, and Superintendent Strick- land asked for a remand until Tuesday next. The dis- turbances were likely to continue. He viols present at the previous day's scene, and there were over 1,000 people of the collier type near the premises. The police had to continually charge the men. So great ass the danger that late in the afternoon he had to telephone for further assistance. It was not until the mounted police arrived that they were able to clear the place. The disturbance lasted all day, and it was with the greatest difficulty the men were kept off the colliery premises. Stones we-43 flying like hailstones. The magistrates remanded the three prisoners until Tuesday next, bail being allowed in the sum of £lO each.

div.head: CORONATION DAY ACCIDENT.
div.p: CORONATION DAY ACCIDENT.

Thelwall Lady's Successful Claim for Damages At the Manchester Assizes on Monday, before Mr - Justice Pickford and a special jury, Mr. Harry Perceva Dansham and his wife, of Cuerdon Hall, rhelwall, sued Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., Limited, brewers and taxi-cab proprietors. Warrington, for damages for personal injuries. Mr. Gordon Hewett and Dr. Eastham were counsel for the plaintiffs, and Mr. Acton for the defendants.

The case for the plaintiffs was that on June 22 of last year Mrs. Densbam and two children were in a motor-car, going along London-road to see the Corona- tion bonfire at Warren Hill. The pace up a long, steep hill near Hill Cliffs house was about floe miles an hour, and as there was a lot of traffic about the horn was fre- quently sounded. While they were passing a trap, the defendants'taxi-cab,which was without a passenger, was turned suddenly and without warning from behind ran jut the trap and into the off-side of the plaintiff's car. Con- siderable damage was done to the car,and Mrs Densham was pitched against the screen, so that her nose was cut, and in addition to sustaining severe bruises,she WBS shaken so badly that she did not recover from the nervous prostration which followed until the End of October.

----- The defendants denied that their car was driven at an excessive speed, and said that warning was given, and that there was no recklessness in passing the trap mov- ing in front of their vehicle. They made an allegation of excessive speed in regard to plaintiffs' car, and witnesses were called who said that the plaintiff? car was travelling faster than defendants' and that its pace was too fast for such a busy road. The jury gave is verdict for plaintiffs, with £25 damages.
