div.head: MR. B. S. TOWNROE. -- CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE FOR
div.p: MR. B. S. TOWNROE. -- CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE FOR
MIDDLETON. NATIONAL SERVICE AND TARIFF REFORM.
(Special Interview.)

The news that Mr. B. S. Townroe, of Warrington, had been selected as prospective Conservative candi- didate for the Middleton Division of Lancashire created considerable interest and not a little surprise in lccal political circles. During the fi ur years he has lived in Warrington, Mr. Townrce has never publicly associated himself with any political party, his interests having centred chiefly in a strenuous advocacy of the compulsory military training proposals cf the National Service League. When the Executive of the Middleton Division Conservative Association were faced with the necessity of finding a candidate to succeed Mr. W. A. S. Hewins, recently elected member for Hereford, they invited Mr. J. Ogden Hardicker, solicitor, of Manchester, and Mr. Townroe, to address them. Mr. Townroe attended a meeting of the com- mittee at the Unionist Club, Rochdale, on Saturday. Mr. Hardicker afterwards withdrew his name and on Monday Mr. Townroe, who was strongly rccommended by Lord Derby,was unanimously chosen as candidate The decision of the Executive will be submitted to the Council for approval at a meetivg to be held at the Rochdale Hippodrcme this (Saturda)) afternoon. At the bye-election, August, 1911, the result was : Sir W. R. D. Adkios (L W. A. S. Hewies (C.)

div.head: Liberal majority 4ll
div.p: Liberal majority 4ll

Mr. Townrce, who is only 27 years cf age, is a son of Mr. C. E. Townrce, of The Park, Nottingham, and a nephew of Canon Townroe, of Lincoln. Be was educated at Lincoln School and St. John's College, Oxford, taking honours in classics and philosophy, and became a graduate of Oxford University in 1908 From his youth Mr. Townroe has taken great interest in social problems. Ile worked as a voluntary hclper with the Charity Organization Society at Nottingham and Oxford and later in the East End settlement, Toynbee Hall, Whitechapel. Af.erwards for several months he acted as sub-warden of Navy Ffouse,ohatham studying naval problems and prt life. On leaving Chatham, Mr. Townroe came to Warrington as private secretary to Captain G. R. Crosfield and immediately threw himself with enthusiasm into the propaganda of the National Service League. He has toured Lanca- shire, speaking incessantly for the League, and for two and a half years he has edited the monthly "N. S. L. Notes." In 1909 he wrote an invasion play "A Nation in Arms" which has now been translated into Danish and the acting rights banded to Denmark and Norway. Mr. Townroe is a lieutenant in the 4th. Battalion (P.W.V ) South Lancashire Regiment, deputy-chairman of one of the district committees of the Citizens' Guild of Help, and a Governor of the Warlineton Infirmary. In October 1910 he was married to Miss Marjory Collingwood, daughter of Mr. W.OOll ngwoed, J.P , C.C., of Mere House, Newtcn-le-Willows, manag- ing director of the Vulcan Foundry. Mr. Townroe is a staunch Churchman and holds the /Bee of hon. treasurer of the National Society in the Rural Deanery of Winwick. Interviewed by an " Examiner " representative on Thursday, Mr. Townroe indicated the bread lines of policy which he intended to adopt in his election campaign. Asked whether he had any previous onnection with the constituency, Mr Townroe said he had occasionally spoken there on behalf of the National Service League. "Our chief supporter in that district " he added "is Sir George Kemp, the Liberal M.P. for North-West Manchester and a large employer of labour in Rochdale. He has presided at our meetings and is very keen on the question." Further conversation with Mr. Townroe did not give the impression that National Service is likely to be made a leading issue of the election by the Con- servatives, but Mr. Townroe is evidently prepared to meet any opposition he may have to encounter on that much-vexed question. "Do you intend to make National Service one of the planks of your platform? "asked the reporter. "I shall not waver in the least in my support of National Service " replied Mr. lownroe " but the fact that so many Liberals in the neighbourhood are already supporters of and subscribers to the League makes the matter a non-party one and, as far as possible, one would not work it as a party measure." Will you raise the question in your campaign? " " I have already said quite clearly that it is, in my opinion,the only solution of our difficulties with regard to recruiting and training, from the point of view both of the employer and of the employed." "Do you stand as a National Service candidate ?" "I stand as a Conservative but, as far as national defence is concerned, with the conviction that National Service will alone give us a thorough Territorial army." Passim"' on to other questions, Mr. Townroe said he was very keen on social reform. "I am taking up a very definite attitude " he said "on the lines of the Unionist Social Reform Committee, especially with regard to housing and land reform." " What kind of land reform ? " queried the interviewer. "Peasant proprietorship" replied Mr. Townroe. He added that he was arranging a summer tour in the country districts of France with the object of studying the French system of land tenure and peasant proprietorship. There was a large agricultural element in the Middleton division and this question would therefore have a special interest. "Do you intend to advocate tariff reform ? " "I shall go on the same lines as Mr. Hewins—a revision of cur fiscal system. " "And what will be your attitude on other questions ? " "Well, as a strong Churchman, I shall be attacking the Government measure for the Disestablishment and Disendowment of the Welsh Chinch. I find there is considerable feeling against it on the part of many Liberal Churchmen. Any Christian ought to beware lest the claims of party or class should weigh in the scales of his judgment against injury to the sacred cause of religion. What must be the effect of this measure on the mutualrelations of Anglicans and Non- conformists—who are the twin inheritors of the legacy of the Reformation ? lam afraid it can only embitter them." " I am also" continued Mr. Townroe "an opponent of Heine Rule, because the whole tendency of Colonial systems of self-government has been to work from separation to unity. They start as independent coionies and begin to feel the need of a central govern- ment, and to give Ireland Home Rule would be like dividing Queensland into two provinces and making one of them subordinate. " I shall take a strong line in support of Imperial federation not simply from a desire to see the map painted red, but because one believes that the British Empire has a great future and a noble work to do in the world. The British Empire alone of all the great political fabrics of the world, has been , able to reconcile social, religious, national and geographical diversities, with a unity which is the guarantee of peace. One believes, therefore, that in striving for Imperial federation one is also helping mankind in its efforts for peace." If MeTownrce were asked whether he would favour the repeal of the National Insurance Act, there is small probability that he would reply, as Mr. Boner Law did, "Certainly." In order to familiarise himself with all the details of the measure, he has been attending the lectures given by the National Insurance .Comm 189 ion. All he had to say to the interviewer on the topic was: "The Insurance Act will undoubtedly be one of the chief political questions of the next five years. It took the Germans twenty years to work out their scheme to its present form, and I believe amending Acts will be necessary in order to adapt Mr. floyd-Greorge's measure to the varying needs of the community." Mr. Townroe had something to say with regard to the industrial deadlock. "So far as one's experience of colliers in G company of the 4th South Lancashire Regiment goes" he said, "one's sympathies are with the miners on the question of abnormal places. For a fair day's work a man should get a fair day's wages. But the tendency of the men's leaders to adopt methods (f Syndicalism is shown by the experience of other countries to be a grave danger to the community, A satisfactory way out will only be found if justice is done to both sides." "And what do you think of your prospects in the Middleton division ? "One recognizes in Sir Ryland Adkins a very tough opponent and an exceedingly clever man; but our executive committee, composed of businessmen and workingmen, is beginning a campaign immediately -with a determination to win the seat. Personally,

while not altering in the least those convictions which Warrington people know I hold,l shall take a firm but moderate attitude in party politics, recognizing that the welfare of the nation must come before the success of any party. By moderation and common sense I believe . we shall find a way out or our present aocial difficulties. Ido not intend to subordinate convictions to popular favour or to the winning of votes. If I believe in a thing I shall say so. For instance,when a Minister is doing his duty like Mr. Winston Churchill at the Admiralty, all sides ought to support him." The Middleton Division embraces a wide area— from near Prestwich in Lancashire to Todmorden in Yorkshire. It can, however, be reached in an hour's journey:, and Mr. Townroe has at present no intention of leaving Warrington. He expressed the hope that none of the ties which he had formed in Warrington would be broken—in fact the many congratulatory letters he had received from friends of different shades of opinion encouraged him in the belief that he would be knit even more closely to the town and its many interests Mrs. Townroe is mcst enthusiastic about )er husband's candidature and has already made the acquaintance of some of the workers in the division. She is, of course, a strong Conservative, having been prominently connected with the Plimrose League in the Newton division.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, March, 23, 1912.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, March, 23, 1912.
WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
CONCERT IN PARR HALL .

The works performed at the Musical Society's closing conceit of the season cn Wednesday evening, were almcst entirely of a sacred character, as befits the Lenten interval, and although there was not a large audieece, as may be explained by accidental circum- stances, it was one which listened to two important works, given for the first time in Warrington. with manifest interest and the deepest atten- tion. It is difficult, and indeed it is scarcely fitting, in the performance of a work like Dvorak's " Siabat Mater' for an audience to break in upon its continuity with marks of flem .ns'rative appreciation, but one felt that listeners to this work were,throughout the performance on Wednesday evening, to a certain extent under the spell a its strong fascination. That so impressive an initial performance, as it proved to be, should have been given in the town, is. therefore, a matter of self-congratulation to the society and an event reflecting infinite credit upon its members and upcn Mr. Crossley's aseidrou training. The whole performance r as, happily and notably, free from seneus blemish, principals, chorus and orchestra shewing throughout a singleness of purpose in bringing about a presentment of this best known and mrst important of Dvorak's works which will be remembered ES one of the scciety's highest achievements. The choruses "Or my Societal. " and "By Thy glorious death and passion" were part'colsrly fine examples of smooth and graceful ensemble singing, and in their qualities of profound expressiveness probably touched the high-water mark of excellence in the evening's choral work. A magnificent choral setting was found for the quartets fi r the piicripal vocalists with which the work opens and closes, in the two numbers "See her standing sd and tearful " and "While my body here is lying," in the second of which much of the enthralling thematic material hoard in the first recurs as a prelude to the final grand "Amen." In both of these choruses there were some passages of strong emphasis and some massive piling up of harmony and melody which made one wonder how such effects were possible with a chorus so dispro- portionately constituted in the various sections of the voices as is disclosed by a perusal of the list of vc cal members given in the printed programme. But, even when tested in the nakedness of the long passages of accompanied chorus singing in the concluding number and elsewhere in Dvorak's work,it is surprising that so good an approximation to balance of tone was obtained. The male singers,and especially the tenors, are numerically small, yet requisitioned quite apart as they are, they carried through most artistically the tenor solo with chorus "At Thy feet in adoration," which, commenicng with a delicious theme in both the vocal and orchestral parts, closes with some rugged and poignant effects at the words "The story of Calvary." The quartet of principals each and all sang the solos and concerted pieces with appropriately devotional expression, and without mentioning them in the way of invidious distinctions, one may allude to Miss Dora Arnell's singing of "All my heart" (The In I laiiimatus of the original Latin) and to Mr. Joseph Chcetham's " At thy feet in adoration" as being of a specially moving aud tender character. Flom a purist's point of view the decision of the Musical Society to perform Dvorak's music in conjunction with Mr. Crowe's English words is to be regretted, for there can be no question that in this form "The Stabat Mater" is largely disappointing in ' that it becomes snipped of much of the dignity, and more of a certain selemnity, attaching to the original Latin text. Mr. Crossley's tempi were also decidedly on the slow side for a work consisting of movements in themselves already very deliberate—the result being that a performance which should be over in about 80 minutes extended to over an hour and a half of continuous work.

Dr. Reynolds's recently c )mpossd chorus "For all the Saints " received, under his conductorship, a rendering that indicated on the part of the society's members a studied determination to bring out in full its point', of interest. And it is due to say that these are so numerous, and some cf them so replete with subtle possibilities, that one fails to grasp them entirely in a single hearing. The com- poser's task has been no light one in dealing, in the form of a purely choral anthem, with the wot ds of the well-known hymn, with its continuous and somewhat ernbarassing repetitions of the word "Alleluia." How Dr. Reynolds has clothed the numerous verses with a whole gamut of tone colour—how he has made vigorous and picturesque use of light and shade and incidentally thrown an ever-changing light on the recurrent word above mentioned, are things to be admired in the plan of the work, while in performance they are seen to be well integrated parts of an artistic whole. The music is distinctly modern in flavour, a..d presents just those points of difficulty in the intonation of modulating intervals, and in the movement and inter-weaving of the different vocal parts as delight a well-equipped choral society. In overcoming these it was clear the Musical Society's members took both pleasure and great pains, and it is not surprising there- fore that, the orchestra seconding these efforts by playing most intelligently the composer's recently added instrumental pat ts, a most effective and entirely adequate performance was given f this very attrac- tive work, the close of which was marked by a recall of Dr. Reynolds to acknowledge the audience's tokens of appreciation. In the second part of the programme Miss Arnell and Mr. James Coleman each sang a song and obtained a well-merited encore, Mr. Coleman responding with a Lullaby of his own composition entitled "Good-night, beloved! " which, given with a tender grace which is always delightful in a bass singer, was extremely pleasing to listen to. To this song Mr. Payton rendered on the organ in a most restrained and musicianly manner, the usual piano accompaniment. It should be mentioned that the society's augmented orchestra under Mr. R. H. Pearson's leadership and with Mr. Payton at the organ, dealt with Dvorak's lavish and picturesque instrumentation in "The Stabat Mater" in a manner deserving of high praise.

When is a sardine not a sardine? That is a question which has been engaging the attention of the Law Courts, but sardines which Mr. Toole used to call "sprats in ile are generally supposed to be the young of the pilchard of the Cornish and Devon fisheries. They are caught in large quantities off the West Coast of France. Other fisheries are 'carried on in the Mediterranean, but :Concarneau in Brittany is the chief centre of the industry. Here the fish are cooked in oil, tinned, and preserved, in olive oil—or at least that is the presumption. But sometimes the sardine fishery proves a failure, and as the public will have its sardines, substitutes have to be found. And as it is with the fish, so with the preservative, which is to be feared is not always pure olive oil. As the fishmonger said, "whitebait is young sprats:and sprats is young errings," but sardines may be anything. The French say there are one hundred and sixty-one different ways of cooking the sardine,Sand when you do not know what fish you have got, how it was cooked, or in,what it is preserved, there is room forlconsiderable speculation as to. the contents when you purchase a tin of sardines.

div.head: COAL STRIKE.
div.p: THE COAL STRIKE.
IS IT PEACE?
MINIMUM WAGE BILL PASSED.

The outlook in the industrial world is more hopefull this week-end, for at last, it is believed, the end of the great coal strike is really in sight. By 318 to 225—a Government majority of 123—the Tory proposal for the shelving of the Minimum Wage Bill for Miners was rejected, and the Bill passed its second reading in the House of Commons on Thursday night amid luud cheers without a further division. It provides a statutory minimum wage for all underground workers and district joint boards to fix the minimum, with independent chairmen; but there is to form of compulsion and no penalties on either side. The Lords, it is hoped, will pass the Bill on Monday, and the pits in that case will re-open on Tuesday or Wednesd ty. Mr. Balfour's attack was of a futile character. He had to admit that the Conservatives have no alter- native policy, and that there could be no displution even if the Government were beaten ! Ferhaps the most remarkable speech was that in which Mr. Brace declared that the coal war had struck the death-blow of Syndicalism.

div.head: EAGER SUPPLIANTS AT THE OPENING OF THE FIRST SOUP KITCHEN AT MESSRS. MONKS HALL'S WORKS LAST SATURDAY.
div.p: EAGER SUPPLIANTS AT THE OPENING OF THE FIRST SOUP KITCHEN AT MESSRS. MONKS HALL'S WORKS LAST SATURDAY.
RELIEF BY THE GUARDIANS

That considerable distress prevails in some quarters is avid need by the increased num`)er of app'ications to the relieving officers of the Warrington Union for assistance. The number of parsons reli. vcd this week as a direct result of he closing of works through the strike is between 358 and 400, involving between 60 nnd 80 applications. Most of the cases, we are informed, come from the Beasey district. Toe increase is not regarded as unduly alarming.

div.head: GAS AND COKE.
div.p: GAS AND COKE.

In view of the diminishing reserves of coal, the Corporation Gas Department is economising in public lighting. This week half the street lamps have remained un-lighted at night and there has been no light- ing of back passages. It is announced that the coke at Longford Gas Works will be reierved for the Corpora- tion departments, and for bakers if regular consumers.
THE FIRST TWO.

div.head: SOUP KITCHEN AT BEWSEY.
div.p: SOUP KITCHEN AT BEWSEY.

In many of the poorer homes wa are informed there is neither food nor fire, the husbanes having been out of work for the past three weeks. Some of the women whose husbands were working helped to feed those who were less fortunate until there was no wage coming into their own home. Then they began to feel the strain themselves. Some of these poor people will share their last meal with hungry neighbours. With these facts in 'view the members of the Bewsey Adult School opened. a soup kitchen on Wednesday. Many kind friends have generously given money, bread, meat and vegetables which will enable the willing workers to be busy for some time. Two hundred are being fed each day and the helpsis, both men and women are delighted to send a little joy into the otherwise gloomy .home. Mrs. T. Pemberton, 115, Bewsey-road is a very energetic member and is acting as treasurer of the distress fund.

div.head: PRICE OF BREAD.
div.p: THE PRICE OF BREAD.

Mr.E. England,wbo presided at the concert held in the Co-operative Hall cn Thursday, in the course of his address made some remarks on the bread question in Warrington with reference to the strike. He said that he believed he had soms. pleasant news forhis audience. Those people who followed the markets would know that flour was rising. Thanks to tbe skilful buying of their manager, however, the Society had very large stocks of flour in hand. They had been approached by several outside persons to raise the price of bread. The Committee declined absolutely at a time of distress to entertain such an idea and they would never in a period of dis- tress in Warrington do anything of the kind. (Applause. This they were determined upon, nay more, the Com- mittee bad deoided to go further and at their meeting on Wednesday night agreed to make contributions if necessary to assist the town at the-present time. They had full confidence that the members would support them in the policy. (Haar, hear.)

div.head: MR. A. H. CROSFiELD'S DONATION.
div.p: MR. A. H. CROSFiELD'S DONATION.
-- Mr. A. H. Cro*field has telegraited to the Mayor from Cannes that he is willing to contribute £25 to a distres fund; if oue is formed.
mellef of Distress.

Sir—ln view of the great distress throughout the country and in our own town, may I offer the following suggestion. All men who are fortunate enough to be at work should make some sacrifice on behalf of our less fortunate brethren and should give Is. out of every 20s. they take in wages to some "body " or ~rganisation which is striving to alleviate the distress that has now become so acute. The Bewsey Adult School are doing grand work in relieving many poor families with gitte of bread, soup. &c. Councillors Dickenson and Too'e have each promised a subscrip- tion of 10s. per week to the fund as long as the strike lasts.--Yours very truly, 28, Arthur street, Warrington.
HARRY NEW.

div.head: " Boss " of the Show.
div.p: The " Boss " of the Show.

Sir,-1 have often been surprised at what seemed the childish petulance of some of the replies given at meetings of the Warrington Board of Guardians, to what appeared quite honest quest'ons. But according to your issue of the 16th the secret is revealed, the meeting is a " show " and it is presided over by a "boss. Cassell's Encyclopaedic Dictionary (page 639 volume I.) describes a boss as' anything thick, a thick body, whether protruberant at one part or not." On page 640 the meaning is further expressed as " Hollow, empty, resonant, sounding in a hollow manner" and illustrated as follows, "He said, he gloom'd and shook his thick boss bead." Ramsay, Poems i. 28J. A boas sound "that which is emitted by a body that is hollow " Jamieson.—Yours, &c, Warrington, ENLIGHTENED. March 18th 1912.

div.head: CRITICAL AMENDMENT NEGATIVED.
div.p: CRITICAL AMENDMENT NEGATIVED.

In the House of Commons yesterday afternoon, Mr. Asquith refused to accept Mr. King's amendment for the inclusion in the bill of the ss. and 2s. minima. He said Parliament was not equipped with the information or material t) enable it to judge as to what was the just and proper rate. It could only come to a conjectural and speculative conclusion on such a questioo. He was not ia love with fixing a particular rate of wages in an Act of Parliament, and the present bill did not propose to do so within its limited scope. Mr. Enoch Edwards (president of the Miners' Federatio..) warned the Prune Minister that this was closing the door of hope of a settlement that seemed to be opened. After prolonged discussion the amendment was negativea without a divisiun. Mr. Enoch Edwards's amendment to insert the distrio schedule in the Bill was rejected by 367 to 55.

div.head: DISTRESS IN WARRINGTON. OPENING OF SOUP KITCHENS.
div.p: DISTRESS IN WARRINGTON. OPENING OF SOUP KITCHENS.

Nowhere will the prospect of peace in the coalfields be hailed with more relief than in Warrington where I the army of unemployed grows from day to day. It is difficult to form an estimate of the numbeis temporarily thrown out of work, but the fact that the principal works have closed most of their departments is sufficient to show that the dislocation of industry has reached a very serious stage. At the town's meeting held, at the instance of the Mayor, on Monday there was a fairly general opinion that comparatively little acute distress prevailed, but since then the situation has been growing worse and in the poorer parts of the town large numbers are below the poverty line and, but for the relief forthcom- ing from various quarters, would be feeling the pangs of hunger. Two of the leading firma of manufacturers have taken very practical rteps to relieve the nccesti- ties of their vvorkpeople and dependents by openirg soup kitchens. Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co. Ltd. were the first to make this provision, and when the soup kitchen was opened on Saturday no fewer than 1,024 persons availed. themselves of the opportunity of obtaining a sub- stantial meal. The numbers have gradually increased each day, 1310 being fed yesterday. The charact 3r of the meal is varied, vegetable soup being served one day and potato hash the next, with an allowance of bread on each occasion. Only a very small part of Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co.'s works is now in operation, and over 1,000 hands are now idle. The Pearson and Knowles' Coal and Iron Co , Ltd , opened a kitchen at Dallam yesterday when about 500 persons were provided with soup and bread. The Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph) visited the kitchen whilst the food was being dispensed and expressed his complete satisfaction with the arrangements. Only the engineering department of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles is now working, and the number of unemployed from this firm alone must reach 1,500. At Messrs. Wands Bros. Ltd., Church- street, between 600 and 700 men remain out of work. Some idea of the loss to shopkeepers and others caused by the continuance of the strike may be formed from the statement of Mr. J. J. Bleckly at the meeting on Monday that the wages paid last week by the joint concerns of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co. Ltd. and Messrs.Rylands Bros., Ltd. showed a decrease 0f1:2,328 on the previous week. Ouly one-fifth of the hands of the Whitecross Company Ltd. are at present in employment, between 750 and 850 having been suspended. Messrs. Armitage and Rigby, Cockhedge Mill, have not yet found it necessary to close doun and Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons. Ltd., are also working as usual. The foundries of Messrs. Wbyman, Ltd., Dallam-lace, have ceased work until the dispute is settled, 220 men thus being added to the ranks of the workless. As we reported last week, the works of the Firth Co., and Messrs. W. D. Houghton and Co. Ltd. Sankey Wire Mills, are practically at a standstill, entailing loss of employment to 200 and 350 bands respectively. The Longfoi d Wire Co. Ltd. shut down a portion of their works, 'affecting 150 men, last evening, but an effort will be made to find work for as many men as possible in executing repairs and discharging other duties outside their usual occupa- tion. The St. Helens Cable Co. Ltd. will close down the greater part of their works this week-end. THE RAILWAYS CHESHIRE LINES CLOSING D •WN.
Unless the strike ends very quickly there will be no Easter excursions on any of the railways. The various companies ancoutme further restrictions for next week. _ _

div.head: TRAMS MID ELECTRICITY.
div.p: TRAMS MID ELECTRICITY.

Last week-end the thousands of dwellers in Warring- I ton and the outlying districts who make euly use of the Corporation trams were faced with the unpleasant Prospect of a stoppage of all the services, the Elec- tricity and Tramways Committee having issued a witice warning passengers to be prepared for thst cntingeñcy. It has, however, been found possible to continue the usual service up to the present, and there will be no alteration this week-end. The committee will, however, hold a further meeting on Moaday t 3 re-consider the position.

• Users of electricity for power purposes have no cause for anxiety, as it is not yet proposed to curtail the supply. The Feeding of School Children. The Educatiou Committee have adopted spa cial methods of promptly petting into :touch with necessi- tous cases, with a view to providing meals for children who are suff-ring through the strike. The various firms who have had to close down their works are giving cards to those employers also have been dis- placed stating that they are kenuinely out of work. When the cards are produced at the Education Oltices,the cases are investigsted and, where nece,,sarv, instructions are given for the feeding of the children.Up to yesterday over 250 cases bad been brought before the authorities in this way and there will probably be a considerable accession of the number during the week-end. The provision of meals will begin on Nforday at the follow- ing centres :—S tnkey Bridges' Infant School, Holy Trinity Infant School, Ws di& School, Hamilton-st. School. Only dinner will b 3 providrd. Nin erous teaekers have volunteered to help in the work aid the 'authorities are a ailing themselves of their services.

div.head: Rev. John Yonge supports the Miners.
div.p: Rev. John Yonge supports the Miners.

The Rev John Yonge, preaching at Wycliffe Con- gregational Chureh on Sunday evening said, we had all become unhappily familiar with strikes and lock- outs in the world of labour. We regarded both with equal concern and equal dislike. In recent times we had considerably experienced their social inconvenience as well as their industrial disturbance. Many of them had very serious and sorrowful recollections of 1893 when the miners cf many northern collieries struck work, and when for a lengthened per!od all our local industries were peremptorily stopped. They remembered the dreadful privation caused even amongst thousands of Warrington working people. He thought it was impossible to over-estimate the admirable spiiit of I temper in which honest endeavours had been made to reach by patient canference the adjustment of the dispute. Now that that attempt had failed it must become their devoutly sincere desire that Parliament should speedily agree upon the necessary steps to that end. For that it became the high and holy duty of every Christian lover of his country, and his fellowmen, earnestly to pray. It was not Cnristian to postpone making our requests known to God until the last extreme when the combined forces of want, hunger and famine were clamouring about cur doors; and then as a refuge of desperation throw themselves upon their knees to pray. That might be only too human, but it certainly was not Christian. A time of national crisis was supremely a time for Christian prayer. The colliers of the kingdom were tightin; for what they believed to be not only their natural wishes, but their absolute right. They were avowedly fighting for a minimum wage,— which, being put into simple phrase was a living wage. What did

that mean, if it be not a tardy but a positive acknowlecgement that hitherto thousands of men who had sought to earn their livelihood by procuring for the convenience and comfort of millions of people, fuel for their homes, and their engines and machineries had been doing so, at risk and many perils, even of sudden death, for wages less than life could be decently sustained upon. That was the ugly fact which came to the front in the present great conflict and one that should make Christian people very seriously and even sadly, think. That many miners tad somehow con- trived to secure something like a living wage in the past was only a case of the " exceptions which proved the rule." The miners having laboured hitherto at such frequently insufficient wages had been simply a case of eons being content to accept what fathers had put up with. But education and the increased cost of living, which told upon cottagers even more than upon villas and mansions, compelled our mining population to refuse any longer to find coal unless they got a living wage. Who was there who would deny or dispute their reasonable demand ? From the knowledge that bad so far been attained the con- tinuance of the difficulties was at the door of a minority of the coal owners, who would not meet the demands of the men. It had now become the duty of the Government to legisla'e for the conquest and removal of that difficulty. They hoped their efforts would be crowned with success. It should be the dawning of a day in which right and justice between man and man, should be splendidly advanced. If the ushering of it in, should creste temporiry ani universal difficulty and inconvenience let them be willing to accept it. If they were to be called upon to take their personal share in mitigating the passing necessities of the unemployed let them show themselves ready. In 1893 there was a considerable display of humane Christianity on the part of all religious sects, and all political schools of thought. Church of England peonle, in the first instance imagined that it belonged to them, alone or 'principally to take part in caring for the poor, cold, and hungry of our town ; but they soon discovered I that Nonconformist people had humone hearts and I could furnish willing hands. Let them, as non- conformists show a still broader charity soda larger benevolent activity. The cry of the needy would soon be sounding loudly in their e trs. The rev, gentle- men then read sentences from a statement made about the coal strike by Professor Alfred Russell Wallace who was an earnest student of existing social life, in which be said "My conviction is that this present strike will drive the government to take the coal industry out of plicate hands. It is a most monstrous condition of things that such an industry should be exposed to interruption or ruin." They wanted a settlement of the dispute that would put, an end to discontent, that ihould establish a permanent social peace, and that should prevent our nation from ever again witnessing the possibility of a few millionaire merchants, or owners of a national commodity, being able to stop, by their actions the ; realisation of the nations will and the progress of the I nations welfare.
